01 Space

The grid of nested boxes, and every transform between two of them

frameLattice.js 326 lines

The constants and the address arithmetic. Pure — integers and powers of two, no engine state. Everything the lattice promises rests on the numbers here being exact.

FunctionWhat it does in the design§
BASE ENTER EXIT R W G
HALF_W HALF_R T_UNIT
TILE MAX_CANVAS_PX		The constants. Every one a power of two, so scaling across a level moves only an exponent and spends no precision.§3
fl.BASE

The lattice constants: the shallowest and deepest in-level zooms, the crossing ratio between levels, the box width, the child-box width in parent units, and the per-digit shift.

  • Every one is a power of two. Scaling by a power of two is exact — only the exponent moves — so crossing a level spends no precision at all, and a box origin costs mantissa bits only for its index.
  • The previous values were neither exact nor evenly divisible: the box width divided by the ratio was not representable at all, so every box origin in that build was already slightly wrong before anything was drawn.
cellEdge(i, j)The one conversion from a parent box into child box (i, j).§5
fl.cellEdge

The conversion from a parent's coordinates into a child box: scale by a fixed power of two, shift by the index times another.

  • Both constants are powers of two, so the conversion spends no precision at all — only the index costs mantissa bits.
cellCentre(i, j)The child box's centre in the parent's units — the exact whole number i·32.§5
fl.cellCentre

A child box's centre in the parent's units — an exact whole number.

  • Transforms subtract this *before* scaling. Doing it the other way forms a large product and then adds a large offset of the opposite sign, which throws away the small digits before the addition can recover them.
cellOf(x, y)Which child box a point is in. A round, not a floor — boxes are centred on their index, which is what makes the origin a fixed point of the descent.§5
fl.cellOf

Which child box a point falls in — a round, not a floor, because boxes are centred on their index.

  • That one choice makes the origin a fixed point of the whole descent. Cornering boxes on the origin instead puts the world origin on a box corner, so zooming into it walks to the corner of every box at every depth and everything drawn there straddles four boxes.
inDigit(i)Is this index inside the balanced range one box can hold?§5
fl.inDigit

Is an index inside the balanced range one box can hold? Balanced around zero, so an object settles in the nearest box rather than the containing one, sitting near the middle and overlapping fewer neighbours.

carryDigit(i)Split an out-of-range index into carry and digit, exactly as long addition carries.§5
fl.carryDigit

Splits an out-of-range index into a carry and an in-range digit.

  • Exact: both operands are whole numbers far inside the range a double represents exactly.
displacementDigits(d, n)Expand a displacement into base-4096 digits plus a leftover. Every step is exact, which is why a slow drag adds up to what a fast one does.§6
fl.displacementDigits

Expands a displacement into whole-box digits plus a remainder.

  • Every step is exact — a division by a power of two, a truncation, and a multiplication by a power of two — so the digits and the remainder reconstruct the original to the last bit.
  • That exactness is what makes a slow drag add up to precisely what a fast one does, by construction rather than by bookkeeping.
  • A digit counts boxes, not units, which is what makes the base exactly the crossing ratio and the carry clean.
digitValue(at, in)How far one digit at one level moves something measured at another.§6
fl.digitValue

How far one whole-box step at one level moves something measured in the units of another level — the conversion that lets a displacement be checked across levels.

applyDigits(chain, i, digits)Add a displacement to an address, with carries. Reports what ran off the coarse end (a real move of the ancestor) and off the fine end (an ordinary sub-box translation).§6
fl.applyDigits

Adds a displacement's digits to an address, with carries.

  • Reports two leftovers: a carry that ran off the coarse end, which is a real move of the ancestor, and a residue that ran off the fine end, which becomes an ordinary sub-box translation.
tilePhase(v)Normalise the object's grid offset into one tile. Guards two live bugs: a remainder a hair below zero rounding to exactly one tile — which made a real drawing unloadable — and negative zero failing an equality test.§8
fl.tilePhase

Normalises a cutting-grid offset into one tile's width.

  • Guards two real defects. A remainder a hair below zero rounds to exactly one tile width when the width is added, because the width needs six significant digits and anything under about 10⁻¹¹ vanishes against it — that is the same grid as zero but sits outside the half-open range every other check assumes, and it made a real drawing unloadable.
  • And negative zero is the same number as zero but not the same value: an offset is compared for equality across a save, across a move, and between a parent and the child that inherits its grid, so handing back a negative zero would make one of those compare false for no reason.
childTilePhase(phi, c, f)The same grid one level down. The grids nest, so the decomposition is a fixed property of the object at every level.§8
fl.childTilePhase

The object's cutting grid, one level down.

  • The grids nest, which is what makes the decomposition a fixed property of the object's geometry at every level rather than a per-level decision.
objTileRect(px, py, i, j)One tile of the object's grid.§8
fl.objTileRect

One tile of an object's own grid, centred on its index.

objTileRange(px, py, rect)Every tile a rect reaches — half-open at the top. Rounding both ends outward turns one tile into three per axis: 49 ms to 258 ms on one render.§8
fl.objTileRange

Every tile of an object's grid that a rectangle reaches, as a half-open range.

  • The half-open part matters more than it looks. A tile is the same size as a cache square, so a square that ends exactly on a boundary — which is what happens whenever the object has not been moved — belongs to the tile below, not the one above. Rounding both ends the same way turns 'this square is exactly one tile' into three per axis, which is nine times the area stored per square: measured at 49 ms to 258 ms on one render.
TileGridOne value type for the three W-wide partitions: a frame's own square, an object's tile grid, and the cache's squares.§8
fl.TileGrid

A grid is its phase `(px, py)`: an object's is `TileGrid.at(o.tile)`, the cache's is `TileGrid.CACHE` (phase 0), and a frame's own square is that grid's (0, 0). Squares are centred on their index.

  • Two range rules, named: `range` is half-open (the chop and the cede cut on it), `touching` is closed (the cache reads by it). Each keeps its callers' arithmetic to the bit, because a saved drawing's deep picture depends on both (DESIGN.md §2).
TileGrid.constructor(px, py)A grid with phase (px, py); callers use `TileGrid.at`, so a zero phase is the shared cache grid.§8
fl.TileGrid.constructor

A grid with phase (px, py); callers use `TileGrid.at`, so a zero phase is the shared cache grid.

at(phase)The grid with an object's phase, or the shared cache grid when the phase is absent or zero.§8
fl.at

The grid with an object's phase, or the shared cache grid when the phase is absent or zero.

rect(i, j)Square (i, j): [p + iW - W/2, p + iW + W/2) on each axis, centred on its index.§8
fl.rect

Square (i, j): [p + iW - W/2, p + iW + W/2) on each axis, centred on its index.

range(rect)Every square a rect reaches, half-open: a rect ending exactly on a boundary belongs to the square below.§8
fl.range

The rule the chop and the cede cut on. Rounding both ends the same way turns one square into three per axis, nine times the area clipped per square: measured, a level-1 render went from 49 ms to 258 ms.

touching(rect)Every square a rect touches, boundaries included: the cache's read rule.§9
fl.touching

A window ending on a boundary reads the square above it too. `TileStore.content`, a child square's pre-image and `LevelMap.tileRange` read with it; for a single point it agrees with `range`.

span(cells)The rect a window of whole squares spans, so its boundary is grid lines and nothing else.§8
fl.span

What geometry is clipped to: every cut in the engine lands on a line of the object's own grid, so two tiles holding the same stretch of curve hold bit-identical pieces of it.

child(c, f)The same grid one level down, through the edge with centre `c` and factor `f`.§8
fl.child

`childTilePhase` on each axis. The grids nest, so the decomposition is a fixed property of the object at every level.

Camera.js 181 lines

Where you are looking and how far in. Owns the active frame and the crossing state machine. Touches no geometry.

FunctionWhat it does in the design§
constructor(lm, cfg, hooks)Holds the active frame, the in-frame zoom and the pan. Hooks let the engine finalise a live stroke and hold the frame under the pen.§5
Camera.constructor

Builds the camera: the active box, the in-level zoom, and the pan.

  • Takes two hooks back into the engine — one to finalise a live stroke before a crossing, and one to ask whether the frame must be held still because the pen is down.
activeLevel (get / set)
set() · state()		A depth facade over the frame id — the interface, scale bar and snapshots all speak depths, while identity is the frame.§5
cam.Camera.activeLevel

A depth facade over the box id.

  • The interface, the scale bar, scenes and snapshots all speak depths, while identity is the box. Setting a depth resolves to that depth's origin box; reading one asks the tree how deep the active box is.
  • `set` and `state` restore and capture the whole camera, and are what a saved file round-trips.
screenToFrame · frameWindow
centre()		Pixels to frame coordinates, the visible rect, and the view centre. The centre is what decides which box a crossing lands in.§5
cam.screenToFrame

Converts a pixel position into the active box's own coordinates: subtract the pan, divide by the in-level zoom.

cam.frameWindow

The visible rectangle, in the active box's coordinates, optionally grown by a margin.

  • This is what decides which tiles are needed and which objects are worth looking at.
cam.centre

The view centre in the active box's coordinates.

  • Small but load-bearing: this is the point that decides which child box a crossing lands in, and whether the view has walked out of its box.
panBy(dx, dy)Pan, then settle.§5
cam.panBy

Adds a pixel delta to the pan, then settles the camera into a legal state.

zoomFactorAt(sx, sy, f)Zoom about a point. Refuses a non-positive factor, which would drive the zoom below the exit threshold for ever and spin the crossing loop.§5
cam.zoomFactorAt

Scales the zoom about a screen point, holding that point still.

  • Refuses a non-positive or non-finite factor. That would drive the zoom below the exit threshold permanently, and the crossing loop would then try to cross down forever — multiplying a negative number by the ratio never brings it back above the threshold.
  • Finalises any live stroke first, through a hook back into the engine, so a stroke is never left spanning a crossing.
  • Then settles, which may cross a level, step sideways, or both.
zoomAt · pinchUpdateWheel and pinch, onto the same path.§5
cam.zoomAt

Wheel and pinch, converted into a zoom factor about a point. Both land in the same place, so there is one crossing path and not three.

_maybeShift()Step sideways into the neighbouring box when the view leaves this one. Pure bookkeeping and exact. Never fires under the pen — that would rebase a live stroke's coordinates mid-gesture.§5
cam._maybeShift

Moves the camera into the neighbouring box when the view centre has left the current one.

  • Pure bookkeeping: the world does not move, only which box's coordinates describe it. The offset is a whole number of boxes, so the pan adjustment is exact.
  • Never fires while the pen is down. A live stroke's samples are being written against its box's origin; moving the box mid-gesture would append later points against a different origin and tear the stroke in half. It waits, and the over-wide stroke is promoted at pen-up instead.
settle() · _settle()
_maybeCross()		Cross and shift until the camera is legal. Called on load, which is what stopped the first interaction after opening a file paying for a whole crossing — 200 ms once, then 0.2 ms.§5
cam._settle

Crosses and shifts until the camera is in a legal state, and reports whether the active box changed.

  • A loop, because one adjustment can require another: crossing down can leave the view outside its new box, which requires a sideways step, which can itself expose another crossing. Guarded against spinning on bad input.
  • Called on load as well as on every gesture. A saved file records whatever the camera was, which need not be legal — until this ran at load, the *first* interaction after opening a drawing paid for the crossing, measured at 200 ms once and 0.2 ms every time after, which read as 'panning is slow'.
_crossUp()Into the child box the view centre falls in.§5
cam._crossUp

Crosses into the child box the view centre falls in.

  • Asks the box tree for that child (minting it on first visit), then rewrites the zoom and pan so the picture on screen does not move — the same view, described in the child's coordinates.
_crossDown()Into the box that contains this one. Nothing to fit to the camera.§5
cam._crossDown

Crosses out into the box that contains this one.

  • Simpler than crossing up: the parent is determined by containment, so there is nothing to fit to the camera. The zoom and pan are rewritten through the same edge, in reverse.
effectiveZoom()Absolute zoom: 4096depth × the in-frame zoom. What the scale bar reads.§14
cam.effectiveZoom

The absolute zoom — the crossing ratio raised to the depth, times the in-level zoom.

  • This is the number the scale bar reads, and the only place the whole magnification is expressed as one value.
levelPointToScreen(...)A point in any frame to pixels.§9
cam.levelPointToScreen

A point in any box's coordinates, converted to pixels, by routing through the active box and then applying the zoom and pan.

CameraThe view transform and the crossing state machine.§2
cam.Camera

Owns the active box, the in-box zoom and the pan. Everything about WHERE you are looking; nothing about what is there.

LevelMap.js 1,287 lines

The tree of boxes and every pure transform between any two of them. No camera, no objects, no drawing library.

FunctionWhat it does in the design§
_addFrame(id, parent, cell, depth)Mint a box. Wires it into its parent's child map and drops the path cache.§5
lm._addFrame

Mints one box: its id, parent, depth, index, derived edge and centre.

  • Wires it into its parent's child map and drops the route cache, which is the only time the tree changes shape.
  • The centre is stored rather than derived at use, because transforms subtract it before scaling and it must be the same number everywhere.
frame · depthOf · parentOf
childrenOf · spineAt · pathFrameAt		Tree reads. Plumbing.
lm.frame

Plain tree reads: a box by id, its depth, its parent, its children, the origin box at a depth, and the box on a given path at a depth. No side effects.

_isSpine · _childIdId minting. The origin chain keeps its depth as its id; everything else is <parent>/<i>,<j>, with #n on the segment when a moved frame left that chain taken. Ids are document keys, so they never change once minted.§5
lm._isSpine

Ids are document keys and cache keys, so a frame's id never changes, even when a subtree move re-addresses it. A cell a moved frame vacated mints a twin with `#n`, and every descendant carries it (DESIGN.md §13, F80).

  • A re-addressed spine frame leaves the chain but keeps its id string, so `_spine` is the authority on which frame is the origin at a depth.
cellChild(parentId, i, j)The child box, minting on first visit. An out-of-range index carries up to the parent — which is what stopped a camera minting a box at index 2059 and making the drawing refuse to reopen.§5
lm.cellChild

Returns the child box at a given index, creating it if this is its first visit.

  • Carries out-of-range indices. An index outside the balanced range names a box this parent does not own, so it carries up to a sibling of the parent and recurses — the same arithmetic a long addition uses.
  • That carry was a hope rather than an invariant until it bit: a camera that crossed while its centre sat just half a percent outside the parent's square minted a box at an illegal index. The session carried on fine; the damage showed on reload, where the file was refused outright and the drawing could not be opened at all.
findCellChild(...)The child that already exists. No side effects.§5
lm.findCellChild

The child box at an index, if it already exists. No side effects.

  • Refuses out-of-range indices outright rather than carrying, because resolving a carry would have to create boxes and this is required not to.
neighbour(id, di, dj)The box di, dj along at the same depth, carrying up through parents. Panning sideways and dragging sideways are the same operation seen from two ends.§5
lm.neighbour

The box a given number of steps away at the same depth.

  • Adds the offset to this box's index; if that runs off the end of the range, the excess carries up to the parent, recursively — creating coarser boxes if the tree does not reach that far yet.
  • Panning sideways and dragging an object sideways are the same operation seen from two ends, and both come through here.
_growRoot(f)Give a parentless box a parent so it can have siblings. Exact, and leaves every existing id untouched.§5
lm._growRoot

Gives a parentless box a parent, so it can have siblings.

  • The new coarser box is by definition the one containing it, so its index is zero and the origin chain stays the origin chain. Exact, and it leaves every existing box id untouched.
peekNeighbour · peekRingThe same without minting — reading tiles must not grow the tree. What the uncle pickup uses.§5
lm.peekNeighbour

One neighbouring box, if it already exists.

  • A parentless box has no siblings yet and this must not invent any: returning the box itself would make every direction resolve to the same place, and a caller ringing the eight neighbours would get one box eight times.
lm.peekRing

The existing boxes surrounding one box at its own depth — up to eight.

  • Never mints. Reading tiles must not grow the tree, or looking at a drawing would change it.
ensureParent · ensureParentEdgeCrossing down needs a parent.§5
lm.ensureParentEdge

Makes sure a box has a parent (crossing down needs one) and returns the edge between them.

_viewCell · findChild · ensureChildWhich child box a crossing lands in — a pure function of where the view centre is, with no history and no reuse test.§5
lm._viewCell

Which child box the view centre falls in, as an index pair.

lm.ensureChild

The child box a crossing at this camera position lands in, minting on first visit.

  • A pure function of where the view centre is — no history, no reuse test, no nearest-neighbour search. That is what makes returning to a place a lookup rather than a decision, and it is why aiming one pixel differently on the way down no longer creates a whole new branch.
_recOf · recordsThe spine's legacy per-depth { s, t, grid } records, read through the engine's crossings getter.§13
lm._recOf

Derived from each spine frame's edge and the constant grid, cached on the frame until it is re-addressed. Nothing is stored here.

makeGrid · grid · tileRect · tileRangeThe render cache's partition — frame-aligned, constant, canvas-independent. It only decides how much work one bake covers, and cannot influence geometry.§8
lm.tileRect

One cache tile's rectangle. Tiles are centred on their index, like boxes.

lm.tileRange

Which cache tiles a rectangle reaches, as an index range.

  • The cache partition is frame-aligned and constant, and only decides how much work one bake covers — it never cuts geometry.
_frameFor · frameForAccept a frame id or a bare depth. Plumbing.
lm._frameFor

Accepts either a box id or a bare depth, so numeric callers and tests keep working unchanged.

toChild · toParent
rectToParent		One-edge point transforms. Cancel against the box centre first, then scale by a power of two — both steps exact, so a descent of any depth is a chain of exact steps.§5
lm.rectToParent

A rectangle, expressed in the parent box's coordinates.

_ancestors · isAncestor
chainFrom · frameAtChain
commonAncestor		Tree walks. chainFrom is an object's address relative to an ancestor — the digits themselves.§6
lm.chainFrom

An object's address relative to an ancestor: the list of box indices, coarsest first.

lm.frameAtChain

Walks (and mints) the box at a given address below a root.

displaceFrame(id, atDepth, dx, dy)The move. Expand the displacement into digits, add them to the address with carries, absorb a coarse-end carry by stepping the ancestor sideways, and hand back the leftover — the only part that ever touches geometry.§6
lm.displaceFrame

Where a box ends up when its contents are displaced — the whole of a move at depth, as integer arithmetic.

  • Expands the displacement into whole-box digits, one per level between the level the drag was made at and the object's own.
  • Adds those digits to the box's address, with carries.
  • A carry off the coarse end means the move crossed a box boundary at or above the level it was made at, which is real, so the ancestor steps sideways to absorb it.
  • What the digits could not express comes back as a remainder, in the box's own units and smaller than one box — the only part that ever touches geometry.
framePath · _buildPathThe route between two boxes: up to the common ancestor, then down. Cached, and the cache is dropped whenever a box is minted — on a seventeen-level document this walk dominated a pan.§5
lm.framePath

The route between two boxes: up to their common ancestor, then down.

  • Cached, because this is called for every object, every tile, every render — on a seventeen-level document the walk alone dominated a pan. The cache is dropped whenever a box is minted, which is the only time the tree changes.
lm._buildPath

Computes an uncached route: collect one box's ancestors, walk the other's until they meet, then list the downward steps.

frameFactor(from, to)The scale between two boxes.§5
lm.frameFactor

The scale between two boxes — the product of the per-step ratios along the route.

mapPointF · mapRectFA point or rect across boxes, one edge at a time.§5
lm.mapPointF

A point from one box's coordinates into another's, one edge at a time.

  • Going up divides and adds the box centre; going down subtracts the centre and multiplies. Never composed into a single jump, because a composed jump upward cancels catastrophically.
lm.mapRectF

A rectangle across boxes, by mapping two opposite corners and re-normalising.

  • Every edge is a uniform scale plus a shift, so a rectangle maps to a rectangle exactly — which is why the erase prefilter projects boxes rather than geometry.
projectF(o, homeId, toId)An object across boxes. For a resolved outline the arcs survive untouched — the endpoints move, the bulge does not change at all — and the object's grid offset rides along. One edge at a time; a composed long jump upward cancels.§7 §9
lm.projectF

An object, expressed in another box's coordinates.

  • A resolved outline survives untouched. Every edge is a uniform scale plus a translation, so an arc stays an arc: the endpoints move and the bulge does not change at all. The perimeter crosses a level with no re-resolving and no fitting, which is the property the whole representation exists for.
  • Hops are applied one edge at a time; a composed long jump cancels going up.
  • The object's own tile-grid offset rides along, because a sideways hop is a whole number of boxes and leaves it alone, and a level crossing transforms it the same way the ink is transformed.
  • Raw strokes and legacy polygon fills take simpler paths through the same route.
phaseThrough (private)Carry an object's grid offset along a frame path. A sideways hop is a whole number of boxes and leaves it alone — which is exactly why two numbers are enough.§8
lm.phaseThrough

Carries an object's cutting-grid offset along a route between boxes.

  • Up a level the grid coarsens and the box centre comes back; down a level it is the child transform. A sideways hop is a whole number of boxes and leaves the offset alone — which is exactly why two numbers are enough to pin the grid to the object through every kind of move.
framePointToScreen(...)A point in one frame, in screen pixels: mapPointF into the active frame, then the in-frame zoom and pan. The depth-keyed wrappers that used to sit beside it are gone; Camera.levelPointToScreen is the one caller and it passes a frame id.§9
lm.framePointToScreen

A point in one frame, in screen pixels.

  • Two steps, and the split is the whole point: `mapPointF` carries the point into the ACTIVE frame - address arithmetic, exact, and independent of where the view happens to be - and only then does the in-frame zoom and pan turn it into pixels.
  • It returns null rather than a guess when either frame id is unknown, because the caller is drawing an overlay and a wrong pixel is worse than no overlay.
effectiveZoom(key, inScale)Absolute zoom, for the scale bar.§14
lm.effectiveZoom

Absolute zoom: the in-frame scale times the factor from the origin spine's level-0 frame to the active one.

  • Falls back to the in-frame scale when either frame is unknown. The scale bar reads it through `Camera.effectiveZoom`, and `sceneZoom` through the engine.
serialize() · load(data)The lattice as (id, parent, depth, cell), plus a moved frame's pending shift and shadow link; the edge is derived and the grid is a constant. A pre-lattice file is refused here, never converted.§13
lm.serialize

The edge is derived from the cell and the grid is a constant, so neither is stored. Frames are written in depth, then id, order. Every kobin-2 write carries it beside its entries (DESIGN.md §13).

  • A pre-lattice file is refused, never converted: converting would rewrite stored coordinates, the one operation the design exists to avoid.
  • `load` adds parents before children, mints a root `0` if none came, re-attaches each shadow to its resident (the resident keeps the cell) and rebuilds the spine.
ensureSpine · reset · resizeGrow the origin chain to a depth; wipe; note a new canvas size. A resize changes no geometry — grids are constants.§3
lm.ensureSpine

Grows the origin chain to a requested depth, in either direction.

  • Growing upward mints a new coarser root and adopts the old one as its child. Growing downward mints origin children. Both leave existing ids untouched.
  • `reset` wipes the tree back to a single root; `resize` records a new canvas size and changes no geometry at all, because grids are constants now rather than derived from the canvas.
cellKey(i, j)A child map's key.§2
lm.cellKey

Two integers as a string. The child map is keyed by cell index rather than searched, which is what makes re-entry a lookup.

LevelMapThe box lattice itself.§2
lm.LevelMap

Owns the boxes, their cells and edges, and the pure transforms between them. No camera, no objects, no rendering.

LevelMap.constructor(cfg, width, height)Starts a lattice holding only the root frame `0`, with an empty route cache and address epoch 0.§5
lm.LevelMap.constructor

Keeps `cfg` (the edge constants `frameFactor` reads) and the canvas size (read by `_viewCell`, never by geometry). `frames` maps an id to its frame, `_spine` a depth to the origin chain's frame.

  • `addrEpoch` is bumped by every re-address; the tile cache keys its stamps on it.
walk(rootId, fn)Calls `fn` on every frame a subtree stands for: the root, its shadows, their kids and theirs.§6
lm.walk

Depth-first on an explicit stack, in no promised order. Shadows are included because they share their resident's cell and belong to its subtree for the selection and the erase (DESIGN.md §8).

  • Read by `Document.maxZUnder`, `Document.removeFrameSubtree` and the selection's status count.
_adopt(f, p, cell)Makes a parentless frame cell `cell` of `p`, its edge and centre derived from the cell.§5
lm._adopt

Wires `p`'s child map and drops the route cache. Used by `_growRoot` and `ensureSpine` when the root gains a parent, and by `merge` when another lattice gave a local root one.

readdress(id, parentId, i, j)Moves one frame to cell (i, j) of a parent one depth up; its id and every descendant's stay as they are.§6
lm.readdress

Returns the frame, `{ occupied }` when another frame holds that cell, or null for a bad request (wrong depth, a digit out of range). The subtree follows through its parent pointer; the route cache is dropped, `addrEpoch` bumped and the spine rebuilt.

  • Only the tests call it; a drag re-addresses through `readdressMany`, which makes a shadow instead of refusing an occupied cell.
_leave(f)Takes a frame out of its cell: a shadow leaves its resident's set; a resident hands the cell to one of its shadows.§6
lm._leave

The shadow that takes the cell inherits the other shadows. The first half of every re-address (`readdress`, `readdressMany`).

_take(f, p, i, j, empty)Gives a frame cell (i, j) of `p`, making a shadow when another frame already holds the cell.§6
lm._take

Sets the frame's address (parent, cell, edge, centre), bumps its `addrSeq` and drops its record view. A free cell is taken. A resident with no kids that `empty(id)` reports as holding nothing yields the cell and becomes the newcomer's shadow, its own shadows with it; any other resident keeps the cell and the newcomer shadows it.

  • Returns `[shadow, resident]` when a shadow was made, else null. A resident with kids keeps the cell even when its whole subtree is empty (DESIGN.md §8, F80).
_rebuildSpine()Recomputes the origin chain: climbs to the true root, then follows the (0, 0) cells down.§5
lm._rebuildSpine

Called after every re-address, merge and load, because `_spine`, not a frame's id, says which frame is the origin at a depth. It climbs first because `merge` can give the recorded root a parent without updating `_rootId`.

subtreeStart(rootId, atDepth)Records a subtree's addresses at a drag's start, down to three levels below the camera's depth.§6
lm.subtreeStart

Returns id -> `{ parent, i, j, depth }` for the root, its shadows and every descendant to `atDepth + 3`; deeper frames take zero digits from any displacement, so the walk stops there.

  • Every target of the drag is computed from this one record, never from the current addresses, which is what makes a slow drag land where a fast one does (DESIGN.md §8).
moveSubtreeTargets(rootId, atDepth, dx, dy, start)Where every frame of a moving subtree ends up, by `displaceFrame`'s digit arithmetic on the start addresses.§6
lm.moveSubtreeTargets

For each frame, coarsest first: its start chain up to the frame at the camera's depth, the displacement expanded into base-R digits and added with carries, a coarse carry taken by the anchor's neighbour, then the chain resolved from the anchor down. A step a mover is headed for resolves to that mover; any other is found or minted in the live lattice.

  • Returns one entry per frame, `{ id, depth, parent, i, j, rest }` or `{ id, why }`, deepest first. `rest` is the sub-cell remainder in the frame's own units, non-zero only one and two levels below the camera.
  • A native under these frames lands exactly where the per-object path would put it; `move.subtree.test.js` checks it native for native.
readdressMany(targets, opts)Applies a subtree move in two phases: every mover leaves its cell, then each takes its target, coarsest first.§6
lm.readdressMany

Two phases so movers never collide with one another; coarsest first so a moving parent holds its new cell before its children ask who holds theirs. An occupied target makes a shadow (`_take`), the resident yielding when `opts.empty(id)` says it holds nothing.

  • Returns `{ moved, shadowed: [{ id, of }] }`; drops the route cache, bumps `addrEpoch` and rebuilds the spine. Used by the drag and by the undo of `moveFrames`.
merge(data)Adds the frames another lattice minted, given in `serialize()`'s shape, parents first (F67).§6
lm.merge

A worker's descent runs on a copy of the lattice, and a kid it homes a cell over from any visited frame names a frame this lattice has never seen. Frames are added in depth order; one already here is left alone unless it was a root the other lattice gave a parent, which it adopts; one whose parent is missing is skipped.

  • Returns how many were added. `_applyDescent` calls it before minting a kid.
ensureId(id)The frame an id names, minted along its birth chain when missing; null for an id no frame can have (F67).§13
lm.ensureId

Parses `<depth>/i,j/...`, grows the spine to the depth, then walks `cellChild` down the segments. Returns null unless the frame reached carries exactly that id, so a `#n` twin id, or a cell now held by a frame with another id, is not minted.

  • Called for every frame key a loaded file's natives name, before the natives are added (`Files._mintNamedFrames`).
isUnder(aId, bId)Is frame b what frame a stands for in a selection: a itself, a descendant, or a shadow of either?§12
lm.isUnder

Walks up from b, true at a frame that is a or shadows a. Tiles use `isAncestor`, which excludes a itself and knows nothing of shadows (DESIGN.md §10).

objShift(below, homeId, F)Where a moved object's picture comes from in frame F: the unmoved frame F0 holding its pieces, and the sub-frame remainder.§6
lm.objShift

The object's table at F's depth (`shiftAt`) is walked back from F's address as negated cell digits with carries, from the frame on F's path at the home's depth; F0 is minted if it was never visited. At or above the home, or with no cell digits, F0 is F and only `rem` applies.

  • F0's pieces are drawn in F translated by `rem` (`piece.res`), and an input made in F is translated back by it before it reaches the geometry (DESIGN.md §8, F55). Returns `{ F0, rem, sh }`, or null when the chain cannot be formed.
frameShifted(F0, hd, sh)The inverse of `objShift`: the frame at F0's depth where a picture read from F0 is drawn.§6
lm.frameShifted

Adds the table's cell digits and carry to F0's address. Nothing calls it.

_homeToX(fromId, toId, homeId, toHome)Decides which way an object-table mapping runs: out from the home to a view, or back into the home.§6
lm._homeToX

True when `fromId` is the home, unless both ends are the home and the caller passed `toHome`: an input made in the object's own frame names the direction itself (F72).

mapPointObj(p, fromId, toId, below, homeId, toHome)`mapPointF` between an object's home and a frame where its picture is seen, through its displacement table.§6
lm.mapPointObj

Home to X: the exact chain to X's unmoved frame F0, then plus the remainder, which is the point as drawn in X. X to home: the remainder off first, then the exact chain back from F0, which is what an input in X means in the stored coordinates.

  • With no table it is `mapPointF`, bit for bit (DESIGN.md §8, F55).
mapRectObj(rect, fromId, toId, below, homeId, toHome)A rect through an object's displacement table: two corners by `mapPointObj`, re-normalised.§6
lm.mapRectObj

Exact as a rect, because every hop and the remainder are a uniform scale plus a translation. Every rect that reaches a moved object's geometry goes through it: an eraser's box, a selection box, a seam window (F68-F72).

projectLoops(loops, fromId, toId)Arc loops carried across frames one edge at a time: what `projectF` does to a shape, without the tile phase.§5
lm.projectLoops

Up an edge: scale by 1/R and add the cell centre; down: subtract the centre, then scale by R (`transformLoopsAbout`), so an arc stays an arc. Null when the two frames share no ancestor. Called by `projectLoopsObj`.

projectLoopsObj(loops, fromId, toId, below, homeId, toHome)Loops through an object's displacement table: how an eraser reaches the coordinates a moved object is stored in.§10
lm.projectLoopsObj

`mapPointObj` for whole loops: the exact chain to or from the unmoved frame, with the remainder as a translation on the frame's side. With no table it is `projectLoops`.

  • The erase passes `toHome` (`_eraserLoopsInto`), so a mark drawn in the object's own frame still comes back through the remainder (F72).
_centre(key)One box's centre in its parent's units.§2
lm.LevelMap._centre

An exact integer, and the reason a descent is exact: subtracting it BEFORE scaling makes the magnification a power of two on numbers that are already commensurate.

frameGc.js 121 lines

A frame holds something (F94, DESIGN.md §8): a frame with no natives and no kids is forgotten at a gesture's end or a change of the camera's frame, unless the camera is in it, above it or left it lately, or an undo or redo op names it; a co-resident of a forgotten resident takes its cell.

FunctionWhat it does in the design§

02 Truth

Every object, its identity, its history, and how it is written down

Document.js 1,418 lines

The source of truth. Objects by home box, the id counter (which is also the drawing order), undo, and a spatial index. Everything shown at another level is a derived copy carrying the original's id — which is why removing one object erases it everywhere.

FunctionWhat it does in the design§
LevelIndex: constructor
_key · _cellsOf		A uniform grid hash per level, with an overflow list for anything bigger than a cell.§12
doc.LevelIndex

A uniform grid hash per level, with an overflow list for anything larger than a cell.

  • Objects are indexed by their painted extent. A stroke gets a half-width margin, because round caps and joins never reach further than that from the centreline; a resolved outline gets none, because its bounding box already *is* the ink.
LevelIndex: add(o, level)Index an object by its painted extent and grow the frame's bounds: the union box, the largest object, the highest z.§12
doc.LevelIndex

A uniform grid hash per level, with an overflow list for anything larger than a cell.

  • Objects are indexed by their painted extent. A stroke gets a half-width margin, because round caps and joins never reach further than that from the centreline; a resolved outline gets none, because its bounding box already *is* the ink.
doc.add

Adds an object to a box's bucket, indexes it, and announces it.

  • A live object — a stroke still being drawn — is kept out of the spatial index, because its extent is still growing and an index entry would be wrong the moment it was made.
LevelIndex.query(rect, out)Objects overlapping a rect. Falls back to a flat scan when a magnified query would cover billions of cells.§12
doc.query

The objects overlapping a rectangle.

  • Falls back to a flat scan when the query would span more cells than there are objects, or absurdly many — a magnified region can cover billions of cells, and walking them is far worse than checking every object once.
subscribe · _emitEvery mutation notifies, so the tile cache can invalidate both directions — deeper tiles inherit it magnified, coarser ones minified.§9
doc._emit

Notifies every subscriber of a change.

  • The tile cache is the main subscriber, and it needs both directions: deeper tiles inherit an object magnified, coarser tiles inherit it minified.
allocId()Ids are handed out in creation order, which is also drawing order.§12
doc.allocId

Hands out the next id. Ids are creation order, which is also drawing order, and they are never reused.

levels · at · _idxStorage keyed by home frame. at is not a plain read: it merges the frame's shadows and settles its pending shift first (DESIGN.md §8).
doc.at

The first read of a frame after a subtree move pays for it: shadows merge (`_mergeShadows`, held while a drag is in progress) and the shift is settled into every native's table (`_settleIfPending`). Scans that need only identity use `list` or `count`, which do neither (DESIGN.md §8).

_forgetIfEmpty(k)Drop a box's bucket when its last object goes. A drag allocates one per pointer event; one measured session had 4,343 empty of 4,369, and dropping them took a render from 195 ms to 23.§15
doc._forgetIfEmpty

Drops a box's bucket when its last object leaves.

  • Not housekeeping. Buckets are walked per tile bake and scanned per lookup, so an empty one costs on every render for the rest of the session — and they accumulate fast, because a drag re-homes on every pointer event and every erase cedes down a chain.
  • Measured on a real session: 4,343 of 4,369 buckets were empty, and dropping them took a render from 195 ms to 23.
add(o, level, {live}) · finalize(o)A live stroke stays out of the index until it stops growing, then is re-announced against its final extent.§7
doc.add

Adds an object to a box's bucket, indexes it, and announces it.

  • A live object — a stroke still being drawn — is kept out of the spatial index, because its extent is still growing and an index entry would be wrong the moment it was made.
doc.finalize

Marks a live stroke finished: indexes it against its final extent and re-announces it, so the tile cache invalidates against the right footprint.

getById · editKey · editGroupIdentity, and the family a piece belongs to.§12
doc.getById

One lookup in the id map, kept in step by every add, insert, removal and replace; the record's `level` is the object's home frame (`_home`).

  • Null for a native of a frame set aside by a subtree removal: it stays in the map by reference and comes back with the frame.
doc.editGroup

Every object sharing one family key.

  • A family is the pieces of one logical object spread across levels by ceding. They select, move and undo together.
removeById · insertAtErase everywhere; put it back at its remembered position.§10
doc.removeById

Removes an object from whichever box holds it, de-indexes it, forgets the bucket if it is now empty, and announces the removal.

  • Derived copies at other levels carry the source id, so this is 'erase everywhere'.
doc.insertAt

Puts an object back at a remembered position — the undo of an erase. Position only affects the array; drawing order comes from the id, which the object kept.

moveById(id, dx, dy)Translate an object's stored coordinates — only where a move does touch them: a member the pen-up walks back into its cell, and old move entries.§6
doc.moveById

A shape's loops are replaced by translated Loops (nothing writes through a piece view, DESIGN.md §3); a fill's or stroke's points shift in place; the attach rect moves with it. Then `_afterEdit`.

  • Callers: `_normalizeHome` at pen-up, the undo of a move entry from before F41, and the op log's replay of either.
setGeometryById(id, geom)Replace geometry outright, with its attach rect, grid phase and table when the snapshot carries them — for promotion and a move's undo. A drag never calls it: a drag changes addresses and displacement tables.§6
doc.setGeometryById

A key present in the snapshot but empty clears that field, so an undo restores 'no phase' as well as a phase. Busts the caches, reindexes and announces with the old footprint (`_afterEdit`).

  • Callers: promotion to the parent level (`_promoteOversize`), the undo of a move entry with geometry snapshots (`_undoMove`), and the op log's replay of one.
snapGeometry (static)A detached copy to translate from — including the tile offset, because that offset is geometry, and a drag that left it behind would slide the object out from under its own cutting grid.§6 §8
doc.snapGeometry

A detached copy of an object's geometry, safe to translate from later.

  • Includes the tile-grid offset, because that offset is geometry: it is where the object gets chopped, and a chop is where a curve may become a line. A drag that left it behind would slide the object out from under its own cutting grid — the exact failure the object-anchored grid exists to prevent.
scaleGeometry (static)Change an object's units by a power of two. What promotion to the parent level does — the mantissa is untouched and only the exponent moves.§5
doc.scaleGeometry

A geometry snapshot under a uniform scale about a point.

  • Used to change an object's units — promoting an over-wide object to its parent level, where the same ink is described by numbers a crossing ratio smaller. Dividing by a power of two is a change of units and not a loss of relative precision: the mantissa is untouched and only the exponent moves.
translateGeometry (static)A snapshot, moved. Never mutates the snapshot.§6
doc.translateGeometry

A geometry snapshot, moved. Never mutates the snapshot, so a drag can translate from the same starting state on every event.

rehomeById(id, toLevel)Move an object to a different box without touching a single coordinate. Neighbouring boxes' origins differ by exactly one box width, so the same local coordinates describe the moved object exactly. Tagged, so a drag does not read it as the object going away.§6
doc.rehomeById

Moves an object to a different box without touching a single coordinate.

  • This is what makes a move at depth survive. A drag used to translate every member's geometry by the displacement times the ratio raised to the separation, which for a member five levels below the camera meant rewriting coordinates to 7.3 × 10¹⁸ and destroying 82.9% of its area.
  • Under the box lattice the whole-box part of any displacement is a change of address: the object lands in the box that many steps along, and because neighbouring boxes' origins differ by exactly one box width, the same local coordinates describe the moved object exactly.
  • Emits a removal and an addition so caches invalidate both where the object was and where it now is — but tagged, because anything tracking identity must not read it as the object going away. Without the tag a drag drops every member the moment it re-homes and the rest of the gesture moves only what happened to stay put.
eraseReplaceById(id, regions)Replace an object with what an area erase left of it. One region keeps the family key — the same object with less ink; several regions is a genuine split and the pieces are strangers.§10 §12
doc.eraseReplaceById

Replaces an object with the regions an area erase left of it.

  • Each region becomes its own object with a fresh id, inheriting the source's drawing order, colour and opacity, so disjoint leftovers select and re-erase independently with tight bounding boxes.
  • One region keeps the family key — that is the same object with less ink, a bite that did not sever. Several regions is a split, and the pieces are rightly strangers. Getting this wrong cost two debugging rounds: outlining a stroke minted a new family key, so every reference taken beforehand silently named nothing.
  • The pen width travels with every piece, so a stroke cut in two still clusters as the stroke it was rather than as two blobs the size of their bounding boxes.
cedeTileById(...)Cede a tile on the document: cut the rect out of the parent exactly, in the parent's own coordinates, and mint the ink inside as kids one level down. Only the tests call it; the erase's descent cedes on a virtual document (eraseDescent.cedeVirtual).§10
doc.cedeTileById

Converts a legacy fill first and refuses anything but a shape. The rect is subtracted in the parent's own coordinates, so every piece it does not cut stays bit for bit (F42); slivers along the rect are dropped against the pen.

  • Remnant pieces keep the parent's frame, attach rect, grid phase and table; kids go to `level` with the caller's window, phase and table (the parent's shifted one level down by default). All keep the parent's z, colour, opacity, pen and family key.
  • The product's descent runs its virtual twin, `eraseDescent.cedeVirtual`, and `_applyDescent` mints the result in the order this function gives; `KobinEngine.edit.test.js` calls this one.
bakeShapeById(id, loops, w)A drawn stroke becomes its resolved outline, keeping its id — and so its drawing order, the selection pointing at it, and every undo record naming it. No undo entry: baking is the machine's decision, not the user's.§7 §12
doc.bakeShapeById

Turns a drawn stroke into its resolved outline, in place.

  • Keeps the id, and so the drawing order, the selection pointing at it, and every undo record that names it.
  • Drops the centreline: it has done its job, nothing downstream reads it again, and keeping both would mean keeping them in agreement forever. The pen width survives as a property of the shape, which scene clustering needs and a perimeter cannot otherwise report.
  • Pushes no undo entry. Baking is a system action — the user drew a stroke, and undo must reverse *that*, not the machine's decision about how to store it.
fillToShapeById(id)A pre-arc polygon fill becomes an outline — only when something is about to cut it, which is the only time the arc form buys anything.§13
doc.fillToShapeById

Converts a legacy polygon fill into a resolved outline, in place.

  • Only ever called when something is about to cut the object. Everything else reads a fill perfectly well as it is, so this is not a migration — it is a promotion at the moment it pays for itself. One recorded drawing carries a 1.8-million-vertex fill, and converting that at load would cost more than everything else on the way in put together.
_bboxNow · _afterEditBust the derived caches, reindex, and announce with the old footprint so the cache can invalidate where the object was as well as where it is.§9
doc._afterEdit

After any edit: drop the derived caches attached to the object, bump its edit counter, reindex it, and announce the change with the old footprint so the tile cache can invalidate where the object was as well as where it is now.

  • The edit counter matters more than it looks: the renderer's signature rounds coordinates, and at the deepest in-level zoom a whole pixel of drag is below that rounding. Without the counter a dragged object would keep its old path and sit still while the pointer moved.
queryRect(level, rect)Spatial query, plus any still-growing live stroke, which cannot be indexed.§12
doc.queryRect

Objects overlapping a rectangle at one level, from the spatial index, plus any still-growing live stroke — which cannot be indexed and so is reported unconditionally.

_undoMove · _invertMoveUndo a move: the frame back first, then the geometry snapshot where the pen-up normalised a member, then the displacement table — byte-exact on the stored natives.§6
doc._undoMove

Each step is independent, so a normalised member carries both pairs. An entry with only `dx`/`dy` is from before F41 and is undone by the inverse translation. `_invertMove` swaps each pair for the redo (DESIGN.md §8).

pushUndo · canUndo · canRedo
undo · redo · _invert		Op inversion. One gesture is one action, however much geometry it touched; an eraser's background work appends to the same action rather than making its own.§10
doc.pushUndo

Records an action, caps the history, and clears the redo branch — a fresh action forks history.

clear · _replaceWipe, carrying whatever engine state must round-trip with it.
doc.clear

Wipes the document, carrying whatever engine state must round-trip with it — the camera and the box tree — so undoing a clear restores the view as well as the ink.

serializeNatives()A whitelist per type, so runtime-only fields never reach a file. The cutting-grid offset is written because it is geometry.§13
doc.serializeNatives

Writes every object out, with a whitelist per type so runtime-only fields never reach a file.

  • A resolved outline is written as its encoded loops, which is usually smaller than the samples it came from, because burial culling threw most of the chain away.
  • Drawing order is written only when it differs from the id, so ordinary files stay byte-identical to what earlier builds produced.
  • The cutting-grid offset is written because it is geometry: drop it and a reloaded drawing subdivides somewhere else, which moves every straightened chord in it.
loadNatives(snap)Strips retired fields, repairs unclosed outlines, drops empty buckets, and never reuses an id.§13
doc.loadNatives

Reads objects back, repairing what it can and refusing nothing it can mend.

  • Strips retired fields at the door rather than carrying inert state that still looks meaningful — a field recording where a hole *should* have been is worse than no field at all.
  • Repairs unclosed outlines on the way in, so a drawing damaged by an older build opens, renders, and — the part that matters — saves.
  • Leaves legacy polygon fills alone. Converting at load would be the one expensive thing a load does; one recorded drawing carries a 1.8-million-vertex fill. They are promoted only when something needs to cut them.
  • Never reuses an id, counting family keys as well, because an object whose id happened to equal a live family key would silently join that family.
  • Drops empty buckets, which is what repairs the drawings that already carry thousands of them.
flattenLoops(o)Turns a shape's plain piece-array loops into stored Loops, in place, at the door of the document.§7
doc.flattenLoops

Every way a shape enters or changes in the document calls it (`add`, `insertAt`, the geometry edits, `insertFrameSubtree`); builders hand over piece arrays and never see them again (DESIGN.md §3). A loop that already is a Loop is left as it is.

  • Not `curveOutline.flattenLoops`, which flattens arcs to polygons.
nativeFromRecord(o)A stored record, kobin-1 JSON or a kobin-2 span, as a live native: retired fields stripped, the table decoded, damaged loops repaired.§13
doc.nativeFromRecord

Drops `windows`, `srcId` and `paths`; decodes `below`, dropping a malformed one rather than refusing; keeps header fields this build does not know as `_extra` so they are written back. A well-formed encoding is wrapped as Loops with no copy; only a damaged one is decoded, repaired and rebuilt.

  • A fill stays a fill; `fillToShapeById` converts one when something cuts it. Used by `loadNatives` and the op log's replay.
DocumentThe source of truth.§3
doc.Document

Every native object, the id counter that doubles as z-order, the undo stacks, and the per-box spatial index. No rendering, no camera, no tiles.

  • Its change events carry the OLD footprint as well as the new one, which is what lets the tile cache invalidate both where an object was and where it now is - the guarantee that makes stale-tile ghosts impossible rather than merely rare.
_noteBelow(o)Keeps the set of moved objects (`_offsetIds`) in step with one object's displacement table.§6
doc._noteBelow

An object with a non-empty table is added; one without is removed and its empty `below` key deleted. Called wherever a table can change or an object enters.

hasOffsets()Does any native carry a displacement table? O(1), asked by the tile store on every bake.§6
doc.hasOffsets

Does any native carry a displacement table? O(1), asked by the tile store on every bake.

offsetIds()The ids of every native with a displacement table, for the scans that must judge moved objects where their picture is.§6
doc.offsetIds

The live set, not a copy. The tile store's reroute, the lasso's moved-object pass and the report read it; the erase's candidate scan reads `_offsetIds` directly.

subscribeOps(fn)Subscribes to the op channel: what the user did, as opposed to the change events' what moved on screen.§13
doc.subscribeOps

Carries every fresh undo op, every bake step appended to one, every undo and redo, every settle and every shadow merge, in order. The op log (the saver), the scene client and the editor hook subscribe. Returns the unsubscribe function.

_notifyOps(ev)Sends one op-channel event to every op subscriber.§13
doc._notifyOps

Sends one op-channel event to every op subscriber.

Emits no change event: a re-key moves no ink. Severance and its undo call it.

A uniform grid hash per level, with an overflow list for anything larger than a cell.

  • Objects are indexed by their painted extent. A stroke gets a half-width margin, because round caps and joins never reach further than that from the centreline; a resolved outline gets none, because its bounding box already *is* the ink.

Uses the box recorded when it went IN, not its current one. An object that has moved would otherwise be removed from the cells it now occupies and left behind in the ones it used to.

The kobin-2 store's codec: a frame snapshot or an op-log entry as small JSON headers plus one Float64Array of geometry, and either as a byte chunk for the cloud. Pure; its spans decode to the same objects kobin-1's text does (DESIGN.md §13).

FunctionWhat it does in the design§
F64BuilderA growable Float64Array the kobin-2 encoders append a unit's geometry to.§13
f2.F64Builder

`n` numbers used of `buf`, the capacity doubled when full. It has the variadic `push` that `loop.encodeLoopInto` writes through, so a loop's numbers go straight in with no intermediate array.

F64Builder.constructor(cap)Allocates the buffer, at least 16 doubles, and starts it empty.§13
f2.F64Builder.constructor

Allocates the buffer, at least 16 doubles, and starts it empty.

length (getter)The count of numbers written so far.§13
f2.length

The count of numbers written so far.

_grow(need)Doubles the capacity until `need` fits and copies the written numbers across.§13
f2._grow

Doubles the capacity until `need` fits and copies the written numbers across.

push(...vs)Appends any number of values, growing the buffer first when they do not fit.§13
f2.push

Appends any number of values, growing the buffer first when they do not fit.

slice()The written numbers as a Float64Array of exactly that length, a copy.§13
f2.slice

What a snapshot or an entry stores as its `geo`; the builder's spare capacity never reaches the store.

objectHeader(o, geo)A native's serialisable fields apart from its geometry: the one header kobin-1 and kobin-2 both write.§13
f2.objectHeader

Writes `type`, `origin`, `id`, then `geo` when given (kobin-1's geometry fields, where the JSON has them), colour and opacity, and only the fields that differ from their defaults: `w` above 0, `z` when it is not the id, a non-zero `tile`, the displacement table through `encodeBelow`, the erase flag with its `bakePx`. Fields named in `_extra` are copied through.

  • `Document.serializeNatives` (kobin-1) and `encodeObjects`/`encodeEntry` (kobin-2) all call it, so the two forms agree field for field (DESIGN.md §13).
extraFields(h)The header fields this build does not know, so a native keeps them for its next write.§13
f2.extraFields

Checked against the `KNOWN` whitelist, which also names the retired `windows`, `srcId` and `paths` so they are dropped rather than carried. `nativeFromRecord` stores the result as `_extra` and `objectHeader` writes those fields back, so a field a newer build adds survives a save by an older one.

pushGeometry(b, o)Appends one object's geometry to the builder in the span grammar and returns its `[offset, length]`.§13
f2.pushGeometry

Shape: the loop count, then each loop's length and its numbers through `encodeLoopInto` (a stored `Loop` copies its buffer). Fill: the ring count, then per ring its number count and its points. Stroke: the point count and the points.

  • The numbers are the ones kobin-1 writes as text, so a span and a kobin-1 record decode to identical objects.
readGeometry(h, geo)Decodes a header's span back to `loops`, `polys` or `pts`, throwing on a span that does not fit.§13
f2.readGeometry

A shape's loops are `subarray` views of the frame's array, no copy; `nativeFromRecord` wraps each as a `Loop` over the same memory. Fills and strokes come back as point arrays.

  • Every count and length is checked against the span and the array, so a damaged record fails naming its object rather than reading a neighbour's numbers.
recordOf(h, geo)A header plus its span as a kobin-1 record: the header without `g`, with the decoded geometry.§13
f2.recordOf

A header plus its span as a kobin-1 record: the header without `g`, with the decoded geometry.

encodeObjects(objs)One frame's live natives as a snapshot: a header per object, each with its span, and one Float64Array.§13
f2.encodeObjects

The saver's frame snapshots (`useKobinEngine`) and the dev report's local extract are written with it.

encodeRecords(records)kobin-1 records into the same frame form, their flat loop numbers copied without decoding a piece.§13
f2.encodeRecords

For a whole kobin-1 document written to the store (`localCanvases.saveCanvasDoc`). Its loops are already the span grammar's numbers, so they are copied as they stand.

decodeObjects(objects, geo)A stored frame back to kobin-1 records, loops as views of its array.§13
f2.decodeObjects

Checks that `objects` is an array and `geo` a Float64Array, then decodes each header with `recordOf`. The editor's restore, `localCanvases` and the report's loader read frames through it; a caller handing records to JSON copies the views to plain arrays first.

geomSlot(b, geom)A move member's before or after geometry as a typed header with its span in the entry's array.§13
f2.geomSlot

The type is read off which geometry field is present. `attachRect`, `tile` and `below` ride along only when the source has the key, so a table-only move reads back with no geometry keys; `undefined` stays `undefined` and any other empty value becomes null.

readGeomSlot(s, geo)Reads a `geomSlot` back: the decoded geometry plus the `attachRect`, `tile` and `below` it carried.§13
f2.readGeomSlot

Reads a `geomSlot` back: the decoded geometry plus the `attachRect`, `tile` and `below` it carried.

encodeEntry(op)One op-log entry as JSON plus one Float64Array: every object it carries becomes a header with a span.§13
f2.encodeEntry

Per kind: `add`, `put`, `remove` and `mark` carry `obj`; `bake` its removed object and pieces; `removeMany` its records; `move` and `moveFrames` each member as the object it now is, with `base`/`after` geometry only where the member has them; `removeFrames`, `bakeFrames` and `deleteMany` every deleted frame's natives. Kinds with no geometry pass through unchanged.

  • An entry carries RESULTS, never a gesture to recompute, so replay does not depend on the code version that wrote it (DESIGN.md §13).
decodeEntry(entry)An entry back to its op, every object a kobin-1 record with its geometry as views of the entry's array.§13
f2.decodeEntry

Throws on an entry with no kind. `OpLog._replay` decodes each stored entry through it.

packChunk(kind, header, geo)A snapshot or a run of entries as one byte array for the cloud: magic, kind, header JSON, padding, doubles.§13
f2.packChunk

Layout: `KB2\0`, the kind (`CHUNK_FRAME` or `CHUNK_LOG`), the geometry version, the header's byte length, its UTF-8, zero padding to a multiple of 8, then the doubles little-endian, so a reader can view them in place. The module refuses to load on a big-endian platform.

  • `cloud/store2.js` gzips the result and splits it into 700 KiB parts; the report's whole-drawing parts use it too.
unpackChunk(u8)Parses a chunk back to kind, geometry version, header and geometry, refusing one malformed or written by a newer build.§13
f2.unpackChunk

Checks the magic, refuses a geometry version above `GEO_VERSION` with a message naming both, and checks the header and geometry lengths against the bytes. The geometry is a view of the buffer when its offset is 8-aligned, a copy otherwise.

utf8Encode(str)A string as UTF-8 bytes, surrogate pairs joined, for a chunk's header.§13
f2.utf8Encode

Dependency-free because `TextEncoder` is not on every test global.

utf8Decode(u8)UTF-8 bytes back to a string, four-byte sequences as surrogate pairs.§13
f2.utf8Decode

The inverse of `utf8Encode`, for `unpackChunk`'s header. It assumes well-formed input and does not validate continuation bytes.

oplog.js 600 lines

The op log on the engine side: records what the document did as entries carrying results, for the saver to append, and replays them onto the loaded snapshots, undo and redo stacks and pending erasers included (DESIGN.md §13).

FunctionWhat it does in the design§
lvl(v)A frame id as a string, or null: the one spelling every entry and `touches` list uses.§13
opl.lvl

A frame id as a string, or null: the one spelling every entry and `touches` list uses.

OpLogThe engine side of the kobin-2 op log: records what the document did as entries carrying results, and replays them at load.§13
opl.OpLog

It subscribes to `Document`'s change and op events and queues an entry per fresh op, bake step, consumed mark, undo, redo, settle, merge, and geometry change made under no op. `drain` hands the saver the tick's entries and the frames that must snapshot; the saver rewrites a frame's snapshot only then or when its entries have outgrown it (DESIGN.md §13).

  • `replay` applies stored entries onto the loaded snapshots, rebuilds the undo and redo stacks from them and re-registers pending erasers with their done sets.
  • The lattice is not logged: every write carries `LevelMap.serialize`, so a replayed `moveFrames` or `mergeFrame` rebuilds the op and re-addresses nothing (DESIGN.md §8).
OpLog.constructor(engine)Binds to the engine's document and subscribes to its change and op events, with an empty tick.§13
opl.OpLog.constructor

`seq` is the last seq handed out; the saver sets it from the store's header on load. The tick is `queue` (items in event order), `queued` (the pending add, mark or put per id, for coalescing), `removed` (objects removed this tick), `forced` (frames that must snapshot) and `needFull`.

detach()Unsubscribes from the document.§13
opl.detach

Unsubscribes from the document.

_next()Hands out the next seq.§13
opl._next

A seq is taken when the event happens, so entries are in event order even when they are encoded later, at the drain.

_indexOf(id)An object's current index in its frame's list, or null when the document does not hold it.§13
opl._indexOf

Reads the list through `Document.at`, which settles a pending shift first (DESIGN.md §8).

_onEvent(ev)Turns document change events into the tick's items: a removed object remembered, a spent mark, a geometry change as a `put`.§13
opl._onEvent

Ignored while replaying. A reset that is not a load sets `needFull`. A removal is remembered so the drain can encode an object added and removed within the tick; an erase mark removed outside undo and not by a rehome is queued as `spent`, since its consumption has no op of its own.

  • A change that is not offsets-only and not inside undo queues one `put` per id per tick, unless an add, mark or put for that id is already queued: those encode the current state at the drain anyway.
_onOp(ev)Turns document op events into the tick's items: bake steps, undo and redo, and each fresh op kind with its seq.§13
opl._onOp

While replaying it only collects settles, to queue once the replayed seqs are known. A bake step encodes at once, since its pieces may be cut again before the tick: a `rekey`, a `bakeFrames` for a frame the mark covered whole, or a `bake` with the removed object and its pieces. An undo or redo names its op's `_seq` and forces what `_forcedFor` returns; an op from before the log (a clear) sets `needFull`.

  • A fresh op takes its seq here (`op._seq`): `add` and `eraseCommit` queue an `add` or `mark` with the index they have now, encoded at the drain; `move` and `moveMany` force their from and to frames; `moveFrames` forces only what `_forcedFor` allows; `eraseMany` encodes a `removeMany` at once; `removeFrames`, `eraseFrames` and `deleteMany` are encoded at the drain; `clear` sets `needFull`.
_opLevels(op)Every frame an op touches now, for an undo or redo entry's `touches` and the snapshots it forces.§13
opl._opLevels

Walks each op kind's own fields and recurses into `deleteMany`'s parts; for an object it reads the frame the document holds it in now, not the one the op recorded.

_forcedFor(op, touches)Which of an op's frames must be re-snapshotted: all of them, except for a subtree move.§13
opl._forcedFor

A `moveFrames` forces only its per-object members' frames, both frames of every merge, and a settled frame with carries plus the carries' destinations. A frame moved as a frame keeps its natives' bytes: the header carries its address and the tables are entries (DESIGN.md §13).

_moveFile(m)One move member in file form: id, frames, delta, the object as it now is with its index, the tables, any geometry snapshots.§13
opl._moveFile

`belowBefore`/`belowAfter` go through `encodeBelow`; `base`/`after` are written only for a member the pen-up walked back into its cell. `obj` lets replay give the object to a frame whose snapshot never held it.

drain()Encodes the tick's items into entries in seq order, with the frames each touches, the forced frames and the full flag, and resets the tick.§13
opl.drain

An add, mark or put encodes the object as it is now, or as it was when removed this tick, so a stroke that resolved within the tick is written as its perimeter; an item whose object came and went is dropped. Moves, frame deletes, settles and merges are put into file form here.

  • The saver drains again after taking its snapshots, until the queue is empty, because reading a frame for its snapshot can settle it and queue a new entry (DESIGN.md §13).
replay(entries, frameSeq)Applies stored entries onto the loaded snapshots, the log marked as replaying for the duration.§13
opl.replay

`entries` ascend by seq; `frameSeq` maps a frame to its snapshot's seq. After `_replay`, the settles the replay itself triggered are queued as new entries while the replayed ops are still known, for their `of`.

  • Returns the sizes of the rebuilt undo and redo stacks and the number of pending erasers.
_replay(entries, frameSeq)Replays entries idempotently, skipping those whose frames all hold a newer snapshot, and rebuilds the undo and redo stacks and pending erasers.§13
opl._replay

Each entry is decoded, its op rebuilt for the stacks, and applied only where a touched frame's snapshot predates it (`stale`). Every record of one id decodes to ONE object, a later record's state adopted into it, so the stacks share identity with the document as in a live session (F70). An `attr` entry is applied, though nothing writes one yet (DESIGN.md §13).

  • An undo or redo inverts the rebuilt op: from the entry's own data where the snapshots already hold its effect, through `Document._invert` otherwise, and a `moveFrames` by splitting merges and subtracting settles without re-addressing. The inverse keeps the op's seq (F71). A `settle` or `mergeFrame` entry is hung on the `moveFrames` op it names.
  • The undo stack is capped at 200. Each erase mark still in the document is re-registered in `_eraseCommits` with a done set of the ids its bake entries name, so the bake resumes where the log left it.
settleLive(s)A stored settle record back to live form, its tables decoded.§13
opl.settleLive

A stored settle record back to live form, its tables decoded.

frameFile(e)A `moveFrames` frame entry in file form: address before and after, shifts, and its settle inline; its merges are left out.§13
opl.frameFile

A settle is inline because one mid-drag has no op to be an entry of; a merge always happens after the op is on the stack, so its own `mergeFrame` entry names the op.

geomLive(g)A move's stored before or after geometry as `setGeometryById` takes it, loops wrapped as `Loop`s.§13
opl.geomLive

Decoded through `nativeFromRecord`, so a damaged loop is repaired as a loaded native's is; `attachRect`, `tile` and `below` are kept when the slot has them.

The inverses of the model before A1's C1 and C3, for the stores and undo stacks it wrote and nothing else (DESIGN.md §8, §13): replay puts an old store's settle tables and merges back, and the undo of an op that carries them takes them out.

FunctionWhat it does in the design§

03 Ink

Arcs: drawing them, resolving a stroke into one, measuring and cutting the result

biarc.js 451 lines

The stroke centreline as circular arcs instead of curves. Nothing here bakes — this is the centreline only.

FunctionWhat it does in the design§
arcThrough(A, TA, B)The unique arc leaving A in a given direction and passing through B. Tests the bulge, not a length ratio — the earlier test was scale-dependent and turned a nearly-straight gap into an arc of radius 8×108, which the browser drew with a huge visible spur at each end.§7
bia.arcThrough

The unique arc leaving a point in a given direction and passing through another point.

  • Both end directions are stored, the far one computed as the reflection of the near one across the chord — a circle's chord makes equal angles with the tangents at its two ends — which is exact arithmetic. Recovering it from the angles instead costs about a millionth of a radian on the huge-radius arcs a nearly straight gap produces, and a junction that agrees only to that is one the stitcher has to be told to trust.
  • Decides straightness by the bulge, not by a length ratio. The earlier test compared a length against a squared length, which is both scale-dependent and far too strict: a gap collinear to one part in 100 million — which is what the spline's end handles produce — came back as a real arc of radius 800 million with its centre 1.7 billion units away. It bows by a fifty-millionth of a unit, so it is a line by any measure that matters, but the browser rasterises in lower precision where the quantum at that distance is nearly 200 units, and it drew a huge visible spur at each end of an otherwise straight stroke.
arcPoint · arcTangent · arcDistPoint, direction, and exact distance to an arc. The exact distance is what removed the last tolerance from the resolve.§7
bia.arcPoint

A point at a parameter along an arc, from its centre, radius and angles.

bia.arcTangent

The direction along an arc at a parameter.

bia.arcDist

The exact distance from a point to an arc piece — not to its full circle.

  • If the point's angle falls within the arc's sweep, the answer is the difference between its distance from the centre and the radius. Otherwise it is the nearer endpoint.
  • Normalises the angle difference rather than trusting either angle's branch: an arc that has been reversed can have a start angle outside the usual range, and trusting it reports a point in the middle of the arc as being off its end — which then returns a distance-to-endpoint the size of the whole arc.
biarc(P0, T0, P1, T1)Two arcs meeting smoothly with both end directions fixed. One arc cannot do it — it is over-determined; two have exactly the freedom needed.§7
bia.biarc

The two arcs joining one point and direction to another, meeting smoothly at their own junction.

  • One arc cannot do it: an arc through two points with the direction fixed at both ends is over-determined. Two arcs meeting tangentially have exactly the freedom needed.
  • The joint is placed by the equal-tangent-length rule — the choice that stays symmetric under reversing the stroke, so drawing a shape and drawing it backwards give the same curve.
  • The second arc is built backwards from its far end, where its direction is known, and then reversed, so both ends are exact by construction rather than one end being exact and the other landing wherever the arithmetic puts it.
  • The joint's direction is then snapped to the number the first arc reports. The two are the same direction analytically, and making them the same *number* is what lets a junction be trusted without a tolerance.
gapError · arcsForGapSubdivide a curve segment until the arc pair is within tolerance — which happens where the pen turned hard.§7
bia.gapError

How far the arc pair strays from the cubic it stands in for, sampled at a fixed number of probes and taking the worst.

bia.arcsForGap

One gap's worth of arcs: a pair, subdivided where a pair is not close enough.

  • Fits two arcs to the gap, measures how far they stray from the cubic, and if that exceeds the tolerance, halves the gap and recurses on each half.
  • Splitting never introduces a kink, because the left half's start direction *is* the parent's start direction — the subdivision is exact, not a re-fit.
  • In practice this only fires where the pen turned hard. Depth is capped so a pathological input cannot recurse forever.
distinctSamples(pts)Drop repeated pen samples.§7
bia.distinctSamples

Drops repeated pen samples, which a stationary pointer produces in quantity and which would otherwise give the spline zero-length gaps to fit.

splineCubics(raw)The app's own spline through the samples, so the chain passes through every sample in the same direction as before — the smoothness the user already sees is unchanged.§7
bia.splineCubics

The cardinal spline through the pen samples — the reference the arc chain is measured against.

  • This is the same curve the app already drew, which is why switching to arcs changed nothing a user can see: the chain passes through every sample in the same direction as before, and only the shape strictly between two samples can differ at all.
  • Drops repeated samples first, and handles the two-point case directly.
chainFor(pts, opts)The whole centreline as arcs, in one go.§7
bia.chainFor

The whole centreline as arcs, in one pass.

  • Optionally skips the how-far-from-the-old-curve measurement, which is a second sweep over every gap and exists only to fill a readout — it was 40% of the wall clock of a resolve that does not need the number.
