arc.ArcBakeJob.step

Runs the resolve for at most a given number of milliseconds and reports whether it finished.

  • Dispatches to whichever of the eight phases is current, looping until the budget is spent or the work is done.
  • Every phase can stop mid-item and resume. Deferring between whole objects was not enough: one heavy stroke was an indivisible multi-second job with no point inside it where control came back.
  • Nothing is published until the whole thing is done, so a half-resolved outline can never be drawn, stored, or cut against.
  • Each burst re-tunes its own size towards about a millisecond, from what the last one actually cost, and is capped so a burst sized on cheap items cannot overrun on expensive ones.
circleCircle(C1,r1,C2,r2,out)Where two circles cross. Rewritten so that no expression ever holds the big radius squared while wanting an answer the size of the small one — the failure that lost crossings once a radius passed about 1.4 billion.§11
arc.circleCircle

Where two circles cross.

  • Not the textbook form. The usual formula squares both radii, and this engine routinely intersects circles whose radii differ by ten orders of magnitude: ink carried two levels down arrives as arcs of radius 6.5 × 10¹⁰ — nearly straight, so the radius is enormous — and is cut by an eraser of radius 21.
  • Squared, the big radius is 4.2 × 10²¹, whose smallest representable step is 940,000, while the quantity actually being sought is at most 441. The answer comes back as zero or negative, so the two crossing points collapse into one or vanish altogether.
  • That is an entry without its exit: the fragments cannot pair, the walk hands back chains that never close, and every piece gets sealed into its own loop with a chord straight across the object.
  • Rewritten so no expression ever holds the big radius squared while wanting an answer the size of the small one. Measured on a straddling sweep: sound to a radius of 10⁹, an impossible odd crossing count at 10¹⁰, and by 10¹¹ no crossings found at all where there are plainly four — which is exactly where the arithmetic predicts it turns.

Indexes the centreline arcs into a spatial grid, a bounded number per call.

Is this point inside the pen, by more than a margin?

  • Queries the grid for nearby centreline arcs and tests the exact distance to each. No flattening anywhere.
  • That exactness removed the binding constraint on the whole resolve. Every point of an offset piece is exactly the pen's radius from its own generator, so an exposed piece reads exactly that and a buried one dips below — and a fragment caught between two nearby crossings dips only a little. With a flattening tolerance in the way, every such shallow sliver read as exposed, was kept, and left a junction with one more way in than out. Measured: flattening at one tolerance left 122 unclosed chains, a finer one left 25, and the exact test leaves none.
  • A cheap point-to-rectangle rejection runs first, because a grid cell the size of the pen holds hundreds of arcs on a dense stroke and the exact test costs a trigonometric call apiece.

Position-to-identity, so two coordinates that name the same place get the same number. Neighbouring cells are searched as well as the point's own, because a pair of coordinates either side of a cell boundary is not a pair of different places.

Gives a position a stable identity, so two coordinates that are the same place get the same number.

  • Searches the neighbouring grid cells as well as the point's own, because a pair of coordinates either side of a cell boundary is not a pair of different places.
  • Endpoints are registered before any crossing, so a crossing that lands on an endpoint adopts that endpoint's identity rather than inventing a vertex a millionth of a unit away — which is how a junction ends up with one more way in than out.

The slicing bookkeeping: bill the time actually spent in this slice, aim the next burst at about a millisecond from what the last one cost, and record per-phase totals at each boundary.

  • Wall time between slices is the user drawing, not the resolve, so costs have to be accumulated at every boundary rather than read off a start timestamp.

_centerline · _chain · _oracle
_precull · _cut · _classify
_stitch · _closeWalk
_finishPhase · _finish		The eight phases, each able to stop mid-item and resume. Deferring between whole objects was not enough: one heavy stroke was an indivisible multi-second job with no point inside it where control came back.§7
arc._centerline

Phase 1. Builds the arc chain from the pen samples, in chunks.

  • Uses the same incremental pen the live drawing uses, so this produces an identical chain — and is skipped entirely when the live pen handed one over.
arc._chain

Phase 2. Builds both edges and both end caps as one closed ring.

  • A lone tap short-circuits here to the pen's own circle, which needs none of what follows.
  • Afterwards each piece is given its position within its own rail, because adjacency has to be judged on the original chain rather than on the surviving array — and per rail, because a closed stroke has two closed rails and the last piece of one is not a neighbour of the first piece of the other.
arc._oracle

Phase 3. Builds the burial index, in chunks, then sets the margin — which now only keeps a point sitting exactly on the boundary off a coin flip, rather than absorbing a flattening error.

arc._precull

Phase 4. Drops the chain pieces that are wholly inside the pen.

  • Conservative: only drops a piece when its entire bounding box is buried. Sampling the piece instead is what once dropped real boundary.
  • Then two more sliced sub-phases that were themselves dropping frames — inserting every survivor into the broad-phase grid, and registering its two endpoints — because a dense stroke leaves ten thousand survivors and that is tens of thousands of operations with nowhere to yield.
arc._cut

Phase 5. Splits the chain wherever it crosses itself.

  • For each piece, asks the grid for nearby pieces and intersects them in closed form.
  • Skips immediate neighbours. Consecutive pieces share a point and a direction, which makes their circles tangent — and two tangent circles meet at exactly the one point they already share. A neighbour has nothing to contribute and everything to confuse. Judged cyclically and within a rail.
  • Each crossing gets one vertex identity, so both pieces are cut at the very same point rather than at two roundings of it.
arc._classify

Phase 6. Splits each piece at its crossings and keeps the fragments the pen does not cover.

  • A crossing that resolved to one of the piece's own endpoints is not a cut — and dropping it by vertex identity drops it on the other piece too, because both saw the same vertex.
  • Each surviving fragment is tested at its midpoint, which is decisive because the cuts are exactly where the coverage can change.
arc._stitch

Phase 7. Walks the surviving fragments into closed loops.

  • Indexes fragments by their start vertex, then follows each chain: take a fragment, look up what leaves its end vertex, and continue until the loop closes or nothing unused leaves.
  • Resumable mid-loop. One loop of a dense scribble runs to thousands of pieces, and chunking on start indices meant a slice could pick one up and follow it to the end with nowhere to stop.
  • Area and perimeter accrue as the loop is walked, because measuring them afterwards is two more passes over every piece and those passes were the last thing in the resolve with nowhere to yield.
arc._closeWalk

Closes off the loop being walked, carrying its measured area and perimeter with it.

arc._finishPhase

Phase 8. Three finishing passes, all sliced.

  • Hairlines first, before anything counts loops or junctions: strips so thin their two sides are the same line paint nothing, and an unclosed one is a fragment rather than an unclosed boundary.
  • One canonical handedness. Which way the chain wound is an accident of walking one edge before the other, and every consumer downstream is easier to reason about if solid area is positive. A global flip is the only correction that never disturbs an outer loop's relationship to its holes.
  • Junction balance as a health check: a boundary that closes by construction enters every vertex exactly as often as it leaves.
bakeArcPerimeter(pts, w)The whole resolve at once — the same job, driven with no budget.§7

`(p − c)·f + o`. `p·f + t` and `(p − c)·f` are the same number and not the same computation: the first forms a large product and adds a large offset of the opposite sign, losing the low bits; the second cancels at the parent's scale, then multiplies by a power of two.

Is a point on the curve a piece runs along — its whole line, or its whole circle? Range is a separate question.

Where two pieces lie exactly on top of each other, as a parameter interval.

  • The case the intersectors cannot see. Two coincident curves have no crossing to find, but the overlap still has to start and end somewhere, and a fragment half on the other boundary and half off it cannot be classified either way.
  • Not a corner case in a drawing app: it is what finishing a cut you started earlier looks like.
shapeBoolean(A, B, op)The boolean, with one retry at a different welding radius when the first attempt lost something. Perturbing the radius moves a discrete decision off its boundary; nothing normal pays for it.§11
shp.shapeBoolean

The boolean, with one retry.

  • Pairing ends at a vertex is a discrete decision made from continuous coordinates: which ends are the same point, and in what angular order. A configuration landing exactly on that boundary — an eraser running tangent to the edge it cuts, three arcs meeting at one point — can pair ends into chains that do not close, and then a real stretch of boundary is simply lost.
  • Perturbing the welding radius moves the decision off the boundary. A tenth and ten times are both still tiny against every feature in play, and the retry only runs when the first attempt lost something, so nothing normal pays for it.
shapeBooleanOnce(A, B, op)The cut itself: straighten, pass untouched loops through, cut at crossings and overlaps, classify each fragment, stitch, close. Cost is proportional to the gesture, not the drawing.§11
shp.shapeBooleanOnce

One pass of the exact boolean.

  • Normalise and straighten. One handedness for both shapes; on a working copy every arc at or over the freeze radius is stood in for by its chord (`straighten`). The originals are kept beside it, and a loop or piece the cut does not reach comes out as the original (F42).
  • Pass through what cannot be involved. A loop whose box misses the other shape's box cannot cross it or be inside it, which keeps the cost proportional to the gesture rather than to the drawing.
  • Cut at every crossing and at the ends of every stretch where the two lie on top of each other, with the welding radius taken from the smaller shape and the coordinates where the two meet. A subject line keeps its canonical line (`cutLine`), a subject arc its canonical arc (`cutArc`).
  • Classify each fragment by a winding query at its midpoint against the other shape (`RayIndex`); a fragment on the shared boundary is decided by orientation. Stitch the survivors, drop hairlines, and seal what the walk could not close, counting it (`sealed`, `sealedArea`).
stitch(kept, vs)Pair the loose ends at each junction by angle so the "next" relation is a bijection — its cycles are then the loops, by construction.§11
shp.stitch

Pairs the loose ends at each vertex, then walks the pairs into loops.

  • Ends are paired before any walking: sweep them by angle and match every departure to the most recent arrival, going round twice so a departure that precedes every arrival still finds the one behind it.
  • That makes the 'what comes next' relation a bijection on fragments, so its cycles *are* the loops — the walk cannot wander into an ambiguous junction and take the wrong exit.
subtractShape · intersectShape
clipShapeToRect		The three forms callers use. Both inputs must be simple, and the output is — so booleans compose.§10 §11
shp.subtractShape

Shape minus shape, as resolved loops. Both inputs must be simple, and the output is, so booleans compose.

shp.intersectShape

The part of one shape inside another.

shp.clipShapeToRect

A shape clipped to a rectangle — the intersection with a rectangle loop, and the exact operation the chain uses at every level.

shapeComponents(loops)Connected components. A hole belongs to the smallest outer loop that contains it.§10
shp.shapeComponents

Splits a loop set into connected components.

  • A hole belongs to the smallest outer loop that contains it, so a shape with several holes and several islands comes apart correctly rather than by nesting order.
wrap(d)An angle into a single turn.§5
shp.wrap

The same helper as `arcPerimeter`'s, separately defined - the two modules do not import each other's private arithmetic.

segmentTerm(theta)`θ − sin θ`, the circular-segment factor of an arc's area, without the cancellation that turns it into noise for a deep arc's tiny sweep.§7
shp.segmentTerm

Literal above 1e-2 rad; below it, three terms of the series, exact to double precision there. `loopArea` and the scene index's area walk read it.

  • A level-3 arc sweeps about 2e-8 rad, whose cubic term is below one ulp of the sweep: written literally, `sweep − sin(sweep)` times r²/2 was ±60 units² of noise, and the erase's grazing test read a 12-px nick as having added ink (F46).
_setRayIndex(on)Probe switch: off makes every `RayIndex` built afterwards the flat scan, to compare the index against it.
shp._setRayIndex

Read when a `RayIndex` is constructed. Only `erase.report.probe.js` calls it (`RAY_INDEX=0`).

RayIndexOne shape's pieces bucketed per ray direction, so a winding query visits only the pieces whose box straddles the ray's line.§11
shp.RayIndex

Built by the boolean over each operand's `flatPieces`; a direction is indexed the first time a query uses it. The answer is `rayCross`'s own, piece for piece.

  • Measured on the same cuts (DESIGN.md §7): 2,630 → 175 ms and 2,377 → 143 ms, results identical. Under 32 pieces the index is skipped and the flat scan runs.
RayIndex.constructor(flat)Hold the piece list, and switch the buckets on only for 32 pieces or more and while the probe switch allows it.§11
shp.RayIndex.constructor

Below 32 pieces the buckets cost more than they save (the fuzz suite's 20–80-piece cuts ran 9 ms with them); `stamp` then stays null and `winding` is `windingOfFlat`.

_index(k)Build, once, the buckets for ray direction `k`: each piece's box projected onto the ray's normal, in up to 512 equal slots.§11
shp._index

A piece is registered in every bucket its projected extent spans. The extent is padded by 1e-12 of the coordinates and the radius, because an arc's box comes through its centre and at a radius of 1e13 is a few thousandths off (F44): no piece that could cross a ray may be left out.

_candidates(k, p)The pieces a ray from `p` in direction `k` could cross: the bucket its line falls in and the two either side, without repeats.§11
shp._candidates

A line falling more than one bucket outside the shape's extent gets nothing. The neighbouring buckets are a margin far wider than `rayCross`'s grazing band; a stamp per piece removes duplicates without a set.

winding(p)The shape's winding number about `p`, trying each ray direction until one does not graze; null if every one does.§11
shp.winding

The loop `windingOfFlat` runs, over the candidates only. With the index off it is `windingOfFlat` itself.

mapArc(p, pt, f)An arc through a similarity: centre and ends mapped, radius scaled, angles untouched; a cut arc's canonical ends are mapped with it.§8
shp.mapArc

A cut arc (F43) keeps its canonical angles and its positions `ua`, `ub`; only `K`'s end points move.

mapLine(p, pt)A line through a similarity; a cut line maps its canonical points and recomputes its ends from their positions on them.§10
shp.mapLine

Recomputed rather than mapped: an end an erase made carries that erase's rounding, which mapping would magnify 4096× per level. From `P`, `Q`, `sa`, `sb` the end is on the line to each level's own precision (F43).

shareCutEnds(loop)Write each cut line's recomputed ends into its neighbours, so a transformed loop still closes bit for bit.§10
shp.shareCutEnds

Consecutive pieces must share their end points exactly; the file format and the stitch rely on it. Where two cut lines meet, the later one's start wins. Mutates and returns the loop.

arrayLike(a)Is this an encoded loop: a plain array (kobin-1) or a Float64Array view of a frame's geometry (kobin-2)?§13
shp.arrayLike

Is this an encoded loop: a plain array (kobin-1) or a Float64Array view of a frame's geometry (kobin-2)?

encodedLoopsNeedV2(enc)Does an encoded loop set hold a cut line or a cut arc (record code 2 or 3), which the version-1 file format cannot carry?§13
shp.encodedLoopsNeedV2

`persist.encodeDrawing` raises the file's version when any shape needs it. Walks the records by width and stops at the first code 2 or 3.

arcCommandFits(Rpx, tol)Is the SVG arc command within `tol` px for a circle of `Rpx` px? The browser rebuilds the centre in float32, off by 2^-24 of the radius.§9
shp.arcCommandFits

True up to a screen radius of about 4.2 million px at a quarter pixel (DESIGN.md §9, F40).

arcCubicCount(sweep, Rpx, tol)How many kappa cubics keep an arc within `tol` px: n = ⌈sweep·(1.8e-5·Rpx/tol)^(1/6)⌉, at least one.§9
shp.arcCubicCount

The sixth-root law of one cubic's error, checked numerically to 1%; at most a dozen or so for any piece the tile chop allows.

arcSplit(p, n)An arc as `n` equal sub-arcs of the same circle; the first starts at A and the last ends at B.§9
shp.arcSplit

The interior joins are computed through the centre. `n` ≤ 1 returns the piece itself.

planArc(p, { ... })How one arc reaches the browser: the arc command while its float32 centre is within tolerance, else as many centre-free cubics as the sixth-root law asks.§9
shp.planArc

Returns `{ command: 'A' | 'C', parts }`, one instruction per part, planned at the frame's deepest zoom (`enter`) so the plan never changes while zooming.

  • An arc-command part never exceeds a half turn (the command is named by its endpoints). `segMax` also splits by length, the Renderer's float32 floor for far coordinates. Callers: `Renderer.pushArcPiece` and the ants' `runPathData`.
chordCubic(p)One arc as one cubic from its end points and sweep alone — no centre, no radius.§9
shp.chordCubic

The tangents leave the chord at ±sweep/2 and the handle is (chord/3)·(1 + tan²(sweep/4)), the cancellation-free form of 4/3·tan(θ/4)·r; through the centre, a nearly straight arc's whole bulge sits in one ulp of the centre.

  • A line, a zero chord or a zero sweep gives the straight cubic `[A, A, B, B]`.
chordArcMid(p)An arc's midpoint from its ends and sweep, on the bulge side of the chord — `chordMath.chordMidXY` for a piece object.§9
shp.chordArcMid

The Renderer stores it on each arc anchor (`_mid`) so the thin-rescale measure counts a curve's area. `chordMath.test.js` M1 asserts the two forms are bit-identical.

bbHit(a, b)Do two boxes overlap?§5
shp.bbHit

The cheap rejection that makes the boolean cost what the GESTURE costs rather than what the drawing costs: a loop whose box misses the other shape entirely is passed straight through untouched.

magOf(b)The largest coordinate magnitude in a box.§5
shp.magOf

What the rounding scale is measured from. Taking it from the wrong box is the mistake that welded an object into 68 open chains.

reanchorCutLines(loops, edges)After a window clip, clip each cut line's canonical segment to the window too, so the level below sees the numbers the uncut line would have sent.§10
shp.reanchorCutLines

The crossings of P→Q with the window come from `lineCrossSeg` on the rect loop's own edges, the boolean's arithmetic in the same order. The ends' positions are re-expressed on the clipped segment; a piece whose ends are both clip vertices becomes a plain line, the chain's own piece (F43).

  • A line wholly inside, or one with no crossing found, is left as it is; an unchanged loop is returned as the same array.
reanchorCutArcs(loops, edges, weld)After a window clip, re-anchor each cut arc's canonical arc to the fragment the chain's own clip of it would have made.§10
shp.reanchorCutArcs

Finds the canonical circle's crossings with the four edges (`circleCrossSeg`), accepts them with the boolean's own `weld` (a retry may have changed it) and drops any that weld onto K's ends or each other; the fragment holding the middle of the piece's stretch becomes K, the positions re-expressed on it.

  • Does nothing without a positive `weld`. A piece that is the whole fragment, travelling K's way, comes out with no K (`arcPieceOf`).

freeze.js 427 lines

The object's own cutting grid, the chop, and the freeze. A frame never cuts anything; only a tile does.

FunctionWhat it does in the design§
pieceSagitta(p)How far a piece bulges from its own chord, radius-free (chordMath.sagittaOf on its ends and sweep). The freeze itself is one radius; this bounds a piece's bow.§8
frz.pieceSagitta

`(chord/2)·|tan(sweep/4)|`; 0 for a line, Infinity over half a turn. The chop grows a chord's box by it to bound a piece's extent without the centre.

  • The rasteriser's flattener uses the same expression (`chordMath.test.js` M2 asserts the two are bit-identical).
freezePiece(p)The chord between the piece's own endpoints, carried through untouched — so a neighbour that has not frozen still meets it exactly.§8
frz.freezePiece

Replaces an arc with the chord between its own endpoints.

  • Never a best fit, which would not pass through them. The endpoints are then unchanged to the last bit, so a neighbouring piece that has not frozen still meets this one exactly — which is the whole of the tile-seam question.
arcCuts(p, k, axis, out)Where an arc under the freeze radius meets one grid line, through its centre — at most 8.8e12 units away, a thousandth of a unit. An arc at or over the radius is cut in its own chord frame instead (chordCuts).§7
frz.arcCuts

Reads the stored centre and radius; each root is kept when strictly inside the piece.

  • Only arcs under the gate come here, whose centres are at most about 8.8e12 units away, a float64 step of about a thousandth of a unit. An arc at or over the gate is cut in its own chord frame (`chordCuts`), because it is about to freeze and the level below inherits its cut points (DESIGN.md §5).
chopFreezeLoops(loops, phase, tol, cells)The chop and the freeze. Cut every arc on the object's own grid lines, then freeze each fragment at or over the freeze radius to the chord between its own ends. The render chain and the erase's descent both reach it through deriveStep.§8
frz.chopFreezeLoops

Only arcs are chopped: a line cut on a grid line is two pieces of the same line. Arcs under the gate are cut through the centre (`arcCuts`), arcs at or over it in their chord frame (`chordCuts`, `chordPt`), so the cut points the level below inherits never go through a far centre.

  • The gate (DESIGN.md §5): radius at or above `freezeRadius(tol)`, and both ends between the outermost grid lines this pass applied, with slack for the centre's own rounding. A stub beyond those lines was not cut at every line crossing it and passes through unmeasured.
  • A cut arc (F43) is chopped as its canonical arc would be and each fragment trimmed to the piece's stretch; where the canonical fragment freezes, the piece becomes a cut line on its chord (`settleCut`).
  • Called only from `deriveStep`, which the tile store and the erase's descent both run. Changing where a cut lands moves every saved drawing's deep picture by 4096 per level (the compatibility note on `deriveStep`).
tileWindow · tileClipRectWhich of the object's tiles a cache square reaches, and the rect those whole tiles span — the boundary every cut lands on.§8
frz.tileWindow

Which of an object's own tiles a cache rectangle reaches.

frz.tileClipRect

The rectangle those whole tiles span — the boundary every cut lands on, made of grid lines and nothing else.

freezeRadius(tol)The one freeze gate: the radius whose bow over a tile's diagonal is exactly `tol`; an arc at or above it is straight within `tol` anywhere in a tile.§8
frz.freezeRadius

r = ((c/2)² + tol²)/(2·tol) with c = TILE·√2. A tile is TILE units at every level and the radius maps down exactly, so it is one number everywhere — about 8.8e12 units at the engine's quarter pixel (DESIGN.md §5).

  • The chop, the tile clip and every boolean use it, so an erase never re-decides a freeze. `DEFAULT_FREEZE_R` is it at the default tolerance.
wrap(d)An angle into a single turn.§3
frz.wrap

An angle into a single turn.

chordFrame(p)An arc written from its chord, never its centre: midpoint, chord direction, the normal towards the bulge, half-chord, radius and d = √(r² − (L/2)²).§8
frz.chordFrame

For a positive sweep the arc bulges to the right of the chord. Null for a zero chord or a radius no larger than the half-chord.

  • The chop uses it for arcs at or over the freeze radius, `rayCross` for minor arcs whose radius is at least the chord.
chordPt(f, a, axis, k)The chop's cut point at chord abscissa `a`, with the cut coordinate set to the grid line `k` exactly.§8
frz.chordPt

The height is h(a) = ((L/2)² − a²)/(d + √(r² − a²)), which has no cancellation. Setting the axis coordinate to `k` puts the fragment's end on the line it was cut on.

chordLineRoots(f, nx, ny, c, steps)Chord abscissae where an arc meets the line ν·X = c, each polished by Newton steps on the exact height and returned with its residual.§8
frz.chordLineRoots

A first-order quadratic in the stable form, then `steps` Newton steps. The chop asks with an axis and 3 steps, and 3 it stays: where its cuts land is a saved drawing's deep picture.

  • A ray can miss the arc and still get roots; `rayCross` asks for more steps and drops any root whose residual is not small against the chord.
chordHit(f, a)The arc at chord abscissa `a`: the point, the tangent in the direction of travel, and the chord fraction.§11
frz.chordHit

For the winding query's crossings (`rayCross`); the chop places its points with `chordPt`.

chordCuts(f, k, axis, out)Chord abscissae where an arc meets the grid line `axis = k`, strictly inside the piece.§8
frz.chordCuts

`chordLineRoots` with the axis as the normal, so the products are exact. A root within 1e-12 of an end, as a chord fraction, is dropped: it would make a zero-length piece.

The stored form of a loop: one Float64Array in the file's own grammar (`ax, ay`, then a record per piece, codes 0–3) with a Uint32Array of record offsets. Builders make piece arrays; the storage boundaries turn them into Loops, and every read is a transient view.

FunctionWhat it does in the design§

lop.indexLoop

Under five numbers is an empty loop. It does not validate: a buffer that ends mid-record is indexed as if the last record were whole.

Code 2 gives a line with its canonical `P`, `Q`, `sa`, `sb`; code 3 an arc with `K`, `ua`, `ub`. The caller passes the previous piece's `B` as `A`, so consecutive decoded pieces share the point.

A Loop copies its buffer; piece objects are encoded, an arc with a non-finite radius as a line. One grammar, one implementation for both formats.

The stored form of every shape's loops (DESIGN.md §3): the file's own numbers, `ax, ay` then one record per piece. A piece read is a transient view shaped like the piece objects the builders make; nothing writes through one, so a move is `translate`, which returns a new Loop.

  • Measured on the 12,844-object canvas: an arc piece as an object was 344 B for 56 B of numbers; here it is 64 B and a 4-byte index entry.

geometry/offsets.js 320 lines

An object's displacement table: `below[k]` for each depth at or below its home, the sub-frame part of every move, carried upward in whole frames. A move never touches a stored coordinate; paint applies the table's remainder and every input subtracts it (DESIGN.md §8).

FunctionWhat it does in the design§
snapDisplacement(v)Snap a displacement to 2^-10 of the move level's unit — a quarter pixel at its deepest zoom — before it enters the table.§6
off.snapDisplacement

Exact: a multiply and a divide by a power of two. Snapped, an entry is whole cells from three levels below the move, so the paint-time remainder lives on two levels only (DESIGN.md §8). The drag calls it.

offsetAt(below, k)The table's entry at depth `k` below the home, or null when it is absent or zero.§6
off.offsetAt

The table's entry at depth `k` below the home, or null when it is absent or zero.

hasOffsets(below)Does this table hold any non-zero entry?§6
off.hasOffsets

Does this table hold any non-zero entry?

cloneBelow(below)A detached copy of a table's non-zero entries, or undefined when there are none.§6
off.cloneBelow

A detached copy of a table's non-zero entries, or undefined when there are none.

tidy(out)Drop a table's zero entries, in place; undefined when nothing is left.§6
off.tidy

So an empty table has one form, undefined, never `[]`.

carryOf(v)How many whole frames to carry so a remainder lands in [−W/2, W/2).§6
off.carryOf

How many whole frames to carry so a remainder lands in [−W/2, W/2).

addOffset(below, k, dx, dy)Add a displacement at depth `k` and carry whole frames upward; returns the new table and the whole home frames that left depth 0.§6
off.addOffset

A frame at depth m is exactly G units at depth m − 1, so every carry is integer arithmetic. The carry out of the home level (`cellX`, `cellY`) is a change of address — the native is re-homed to the neighbour cell, and nothing is ever added to a stored coordinate (F41, F55). The input table is not touched.

shiftAt(below, k0)The table's translation at depth `k0` below the home, split into whole cells per depth, whole home frames, and the sub-frame remainder.§6
off.shiftAt

Returns `{ digits, carry, rem }`: `digits[m]` the cells at depth m (1 to `k0`), `carry` the home frames, `rem` in [−W/2, W/2) at `k0` — what paint applies and inputs subtract. Above the home (`k0` < 0) only `rem` is set.

  • Digits and remainders from entries at or above `k0` are exact (the snap); deeper entries add exact power-of-two fractions, and only their sum can round, in paint's own precision.
hasDigits(sh)Does a `shiftAt` result move the picture by any whole frame?§6
off.hasDigits

When it does not, `LevelMap` reads the picture from the object's own frame and applies only the remainder.

residual(below, k0)The translation paint applies to an object's picture at depth `k0` (`piece.res`): the sub-frame remainder, or null when it is zero.§6
off.residual

The whole-frame part is the object's address at that level (`LevelMap.objShift`), not a translation.

shiftDown(below, k)The table of a kid `k` levels below its parent: the parent's entries at or above the kid's level folded into its `below[0]`, the deeper ones moved up by `k`.§6
off.shiftDown

Only the folded entries' remainder enters the table; their whole frames are the kid's address. Folding the deeper entries into `below[0]` too counted the displacement twice — measured as an erase at the drag's level missing the moved ink by exactly the remainder. Used by the cede and by scaling down.

shiftUp(below)The table of the same object promoted one level up: every entry one depth deeper, the home level's included.§6
off.shiftUp

The table of the same object promoted one level up: every entry one depth deeper, the home level's included.

sameShift(a, b)Are two frame shifts (`[x, y]` or null) equal?§6
off.sameShift

A shift is the k = 0 entry a moved frame owes its natives (DESIGN.md §8); the subtree drag and the pointer-up compare them.

sameBelow(a, b)Do two tables hold the same non-zero entries, absent and zero counting as equal?§6
off.sameBelow

Do two tables hold the same non-zero entries, absent and zero counting as equal?

encodeBelow(below)A table in its file form, `[[k, ox, oy], ...]`, or undefined when it is empty.§13
off.encodeBelow

The form the snapshot, the op log and the phone report carry.

decodeBelow(raw)A table back from its file form; throws on a malformed entry rather than guessing.§13
off.decodeBelow

The file loader validates first.

geometry/chordMath.js 128 lines

The arc identities written from an arc's two ends and its sweep, never its centre: bulge, midpoint, sagitta and the area term. A leaf the raster worker imports; `arcShape.chordArcMid` and `freeze.pieceSagitta` call the same expressions.

FunctionWhat it does in the design§
bulgeK(sweep)The bulge coefficient of a sweep, `tan(sweep/4)/2`: an arc's sagitta is its chord's length times this.§9
chm.bulgeK

Each bisection halves the sweep exactly, so the rasteriser's flattener computes one `tan` per depth for every pair at that depth. `tan(sweep/2)/2` has the same shape and twice the bulge — the error `chordMath.test.js` M1 catches.

chordMidK(ax, ay, bx, by, k, out)An arc's midpoint from its two ends and the bulge coefficient of its sweep, written into `out`: the chord's midpoint pushed off the chord by the sagitta.§9
chm.chordMidK

A positive sweep is anticlockwise and bulges to the right of the chord, n̂ = (u_y, −u_x); reversed, every arc bulges the wrong way. Allocates nothing, because the flattener calls it once per chord in the worker's inner loop.

chordMidXY(ax, ay, bx, by, sweep, out)An arc's midpoint from its ends and its sweep: `chordMidK` at `bulgeK(sweep)`.§9
chm.chordMidXY

The expression `arcShape.chordArcMid` uses for a piece object.

sagittaOf(ax, ay, bx, by, sweep)How far an arc bulges from its own chord, `(|chord|/2)·|tan(sweep/4)|`, with no centre and no radius.§9
chm.sagittaOf

0 for a zero sweep; Infinity over half a turn rather than a tangent about to change sign. Shared by the chop's box (`freeze.pieceSagitta`) and the rasteriser's flattener and packer.

segRatio(theta)`(θ − sin θ)/(1 − cos θ)` without either cancellation: a series below 1e-2 rad, and the denominator written as 2·sin²(θ/2).§9
chm.segRatio

Written literally, `1 − cos θ` rounds to 0 near a whole turn and the ratio comes back Infinity. Measured against the radius form at r = 40: 5.4e-16 relative at worst for 2π − |θ| from 0.1 down to 1e-15, where the literal form is 0.08 % out at 1e-7 and Infinity below 1.5e-8 (M3).

arcAreaTerm(ax, ay, bx, by, sweep)What one arc adds to a ring's shoelace sum beyond its chord, `r²(θ − sin θ)`, written from the chord and the sweep alone.§9
chm.arcAreaTerm

`(|chord|²/2)·segRatio(θ)`. A whole turn returns 0, because its ends coincide and the chord carries no radius: a caller summing a ring must take a full circle from its centre, `2πr²` signed by the sweep, or the ring has no area and no winding sign (`rasterCore.itemShoelace`, D60).

04 Views

Turning objects at other levels into something paintable, and painting it

derive.js 738 lines

Pure one-step bake maths. No camera, no cache ownership — everything is a function of its inputs.

FunctionWhat it does in the design§
bboxOf(o, live)An object's extent in its own frame, cached — exact for a resolved outline, bulges included.§9
der.bboxOf

An object's extent in its own coordinates, cached on the object.

  • Exact for a resolved outline, bulges included — a chord-only box would understate a half-turn end cap by the whole pen radius.
shapeTol · freezeTolThe quarter pixel, in a level's own units at its deepest zoom. Deliberately the same number, so the swap of source of truth cannot be seen at the moment it happens. Depend on the config and nothing else.§3 §8
der.shapeTol

The quarter-pixel budget, expressed in a level's own units at its deepest in-level zoom — the worst case that level ever shows.

  • The flattening tolerance and the curve-becomes-a-line threshold are deliberately the same number: a freeze is a swap of source of truth, and it must never be coarser than the flattening the renderer is already doing, or the swap would be visible at the moment it happened.
  • Depends on the config and nothing else — not the canvas, not the tile, not the camera — which is what makes freezing happen at the same time every time a shape is baked.
tilePhaseOf(o)An object's cutting-grid offset, or the frame-aligned default.§8
der.tilePhaseOf

An object's cutting-grid offset, or the frame-aligned default for an object that has never been moved.

shapeRingsInRect(loops, rect, tol)One outline's contribution to one tile, as polygons. Clip first, flatten after — the reverse would tessellate the whole perimeter before throwing nearly all of it away. Two fast paths: nothing reaching the tile is settled by one inside/outside query, and a shape wholly inside has nothing to clip.§9
der.shapeRingsInRect

One outline's contribution to one tile, as polygons.

  • Clips first, flattens after. The other order would tessellate the entire perimeter at this level's fidelity before throwing nearly all of it away, and magnification makes that ruinous — a magnified radius needs many times the steps for the same accuracy, so a 2,000-piece perimeter becomes ~120,000 vertices per tile.
  • Two fast paths. If no piece of the perimeter reaches the tile, one inside-outside query settles whether the tile is flooded or empty, with no boolean at all. If the whole shape lies inside the tile there is nothing to clip — the common case for anything shown from a finer level, and worth 5.5 ms per tile per member down to 0.2 on a real drag.
  • Works local to the tile and translates back, so precision follows the tile's own size rather than how far it sits from the origin.
shapeLoopsInRect(loops, rect)The same clip handing back arcs: clipping an exact arc gives an exact sub-arc, so what a tile holds — and the next level inherits — stays exact.§9
der.shapeLoopsInRect

One outline's contribution to one tile as arc loops, with `shapeRingsInRect`'s two fast paths: nothing reaching the tile is settled by one winding query (a covering quad or nothing), and a shape wholly inside comes back unclipped. Works local to the tile and translates back.

  • A tile is built from its parent's tile, so a polygon here would become the object one level down: measured before arcs were carried, a 42-arc stroke became a 793-point polygon one level down and a five-point one two levels down, its painted edge 263 px out.
  • Clipping an exact arc gives an exact sub-arc, so the clip adds no approximation; the only change of representation along the chain is the freeze in `chopFreezeLoops`.
displayChords · flatChordsCached flattenings of a centreline at fixed, view-independent fidelities, so every tile cuts the same vertices at shared grid lines and fill seams stay exact.§9
der.displayChords

Cached flattenings of a centreline at fixed fidelities.

  • View-independent by design, so every tile of a level cuts the same chord vertices at the shared grid lines however and whenever it happens to be built — which is what keeps fill seams exact between neighbouring tiles.
seamPadFor · seamPad · padRect
SEAMS · LEGACY_SEAMS		One seam policy, absolute and config-derived. The old one was a fraction of the tile, so the overlap depended on the canvas the grid happened to be captured at — 0.48 px on a small screen, under the one pixel it exists to cover. The legacy rule survives only so the previous engine can still be golden-compared.§8
der.seamPad

How far a piece may reach past its own tile, so anti-aliasing leaves no hairline between neighbours.

  • Absolute and derived from the config, measured where a tile is smallest on screen. It used to be a fraction of the tile, which made the overlap depend on the canvas size the grid happened to be captured at: 0.96 px on a desktop and 0.48 px on a small screen — a visible hairline on exactly the screens least able to hide it, and under the one pixel it exists to cover even on desktop.
  • Returns zero for translucent ink when opacity grouping is off, because overlap would double-darken and the hairline is then the lesser evil.
rectSubtract(rect, holes)A rect minus axis-aligned holes, as up to four rects. Pure float, deliberately.§10
der.rectSubtract

A rectangle minus axis-aligned holes, as up to four disjoint rectangles.

  • Pure floating point, deliberately: an integer difference would quantise the hole back onto a grid, which is the whole thing re-homing exists to avoid.
bandRings(...)The one place a stroke's painted band becomes rings, so the eraser's edge and the ink's edge are one definition. In the engine every band is the windowed analytic strip; the Clipper offset runs only for the golden compare against V0 (legacyOffset).§9
der.bandRings

Flattens a curved centreline (only the annulus that can shape the window, when the stroke is magnified far past it), optionally decimates, clips it to the window and offsets each run with `strokeStripNear`, clipping the rings to `clipRect`. Works relative to an origin at the window's centre. Called by `deriveStep` for strokes over the size gate.

  • Under `legacyOffset`, and not magnified, it offsets the whole centreline with Clipper instead (`strokeOutline`) — the V0 path, which the engine's config never takes. That offset goes quadratic in self-intersections (one 1,321-point stroke measured 583 s).
  • For a magnified curve the flatten window must be the clip rectangle, not the width-grown one: grown, the prune collapses and the recursion runs away (measured: millions of nodes, out of memory).
classifyUp(o, s, t, rect, cfg)Empty, solid, or edge. Deciding "solid" is what lets a tile-flooding object be replaced by four corners.§9
der.classifyUp

Sorts one object against one tile into empty, solid, or edge.

  • Every question is asked over the padded tile, because that is the rectangle about to be painted: a solid rectangle is emitted padded, so ink just outside the tile but inside the pad would otherwise be invisible to the classifier.
  • Padding is used at its maximum regardless of opacity, because classifying something as edge that could have been solid only costs a little work, while the reverse paints over detail.
  • A resolved outline is always edge: the clip decides covered-versus-cut exactly, with one inside-outside query, so there is nothing for a heuristic to add.
solidQuad(o, rect, opts)That four-cornered stand-in, overlapped into its neighbours. This is what bounds the magnify chain — geometry can never outgrow a tile.§9
der.solidQuad

The four-cornered rectangle a flooding object is replaced by, overlapped into its neighbours.

  • Four vertices forever — this is what bounds the magnify chain, and stops geometry outgrowing the tile that holds it.
deriveStep(parentObjs, s, t, rect, ...)One step of the chain, and the only place the chop and the freeze happen. Transform about the cell centre, chop and freeze on the object's grid, clip to its tiles grown by the seam pad, and size-gate wide strokes into outlines.§8 §9
der.deriveStep

One step of the magnify chain: every parent object's contribution to one child tile.

  • Culls on the transformed box before any geometry. Transforms a shape about the child cell's centre (`transformLoopsAbout`), so magnification is exact; no move offset enters the hop (F55).
  • Chops and freezes on the object's own tile grid (`chopFreezeLoops`) and clips to the object's own tiles grown by the seam pad, never to the cache square, so two squares holding the same stretch hold the same bits. The tile window comes from the bare square.
  • Size-gates strokes: wide ones become bands (`bandRings`), the rest stay strokes with their centreline clipped past the padded tile. The tile store and the erase's descent both run it; every deep picture in a saved drawing is derived here, so a change is a compatibility event (the note above the function).
projectNative · levelFactorThe depth-integer facade, kept so the previous engine can still be compared byte for byte.
der.projectNative

The depth-integer projection and scale factor, kept so the previous engine can still be compared against byte for byte — the discipline of generalising and then proving the original parameters give the original answer.

projectedSizePx(o, f, cfg)An object's size at a level's deepest zoom — the view-independent cull and fade measure, so the verdict does not flicker as the camera moves.§9
der.projectedSizePx

An object's on-screen size at a level's deepest in-level zoom.

  • View-independent by design: this is the cull and fade measure, and a measure that moved with the camera would make content flicker in and out as you zoomed.
freezeR(cfg)The freeze radius at the engine's tolerance — the gate the chop, the tile clip and every boolean share.§8
der.freezeR

`freezeRadius(freezeTol(cfg))`. Handed to the boolean by the erase (`_boolOpts`) and by the tile store's shape clip, so a cut stands in for an arc by its chord exactly when the chain would freeze it.

TileStore.js 863 lines

The cache of what other levels look like, in both directions. The active level's own objects are never cached — they are drawn live.

FunctionWhat it does in the design§
constructor · destroySubscribes to the document, so every change patches the cache.§9
TileStore.constructor

Builds the cache and subscribes to the document, so every change patches or invalidates the tiles that could hold it. Destroying unsubscribes and drops everything.

setOpacityGroups · bumpEpochA policy change invalidates everything at once.§9
ts.setOpacityGroups

A policy change invalidates the whole cache at once: `bumpEpoch` moves the epoch counter and clears the map, and a tile stamped with an old epoch fails its check.

setBatch(on)During a drag, a tile the camera cannot see is dropped rather than patched — it is stale either way, and rebuilding it later only happens if the camera goes back. Worth 105 ms of each 130 ms pointer event on a nine-member family.§9
ts.setBatch

Turns on drag mode: a tile the camera cannot see is dropped rather than patched.

  • A change normally patches every cached tile that could hold the object, because one edit is cheaper to patch in than to re-derive. A drag is not one edit — it is one per pointer event per member, and patching a tile nobody is looking at is work thrown away sixty times a second.
  • Measured on a nine-member family with 5,810 arc pieces and 45 cached tiles: 105 ms of the 130 ms each pointer event cost. Visible tiles are still patched, so what the user is watching stays exact.
_depth · _minContentDepthBounds, so a direction with no content costs nothing.§9
ts._depth

`_depth` is a frame's depth, 0 when unknown. `_minContentDepth` is the shallowest depth any frame with natives has, which lets `_bakeUp` return nothing when the parent is coarser than all content.

content(F, windowRect)Everything to draw at this frame: the magnified and minified tiles covering the window. Pins what is visible, then evicts.§9
ownContent(F)The active frame's own objects — a plain read, and that is the whole point of cutting a ceded tile out of the parent rather than recording a rectangle over it.§9 §10
_ensureUp · _bakeUp(F, i, j)The magnify chain. Build this tile from the parent's tiles, plus the parent's own objects, plus the ring of neighbours. Chained one level at a time, because a composed jump upward cancels.§9
ts._ensureUp

Returns a magnify tile, building it when the cache misses, the epoch moved, or the address sequence of the frame and its ancestors (`chainSeq`) changed. The bake runs through `_bakeSettled`, so a settle under it re-runs it (F78).

  • Pins the tile before baking, so the recursion through the parent's tiles cannot evict it.
ts._bakeUp

Builds one tile of coarser ink magnified into this box. The chain.

  • Collects what the parent looks like over this tile's pre-image: the parent's own magnify tiles (recursively — this is the chain, one level at a time), the parent's own objects, and the objects of the eight boxes around the parent.
  • Classifies each into empty, solid, or edge. Solid means one object floods the whole tile with no edge in it, and is replaced by a four-cornered rectangle — which is what stops geometry outgrowing a tile and bounds the whole chain.
  • Edge content goes through the one-step derivation, which is where the chop, the freeze and the clip happen.
  • Returns nothing at all when nothing coarser than the parent has any content, which is the common case near the top of a drawing.
_ringNatives(parentId, rect)The uncle pickup: the eight neighbouring boxes' objects at every step. Invariant 2 is what makes it complete, and neighbouring origins differ by whole boxes so the translation is exact.§5 §9
ts._ringNatives

Picks up the objects of the eight boxes surrounding the parent, translated into the parent's coordinates.

  • The uncle. A box is about three screens across, so zooming in slightly off-centre shifts the camera to the next box along, and ink that is right there on screen becomes a *sibling of your ancestor* — coarser than you, but not above you. The magnify chain skipped it and the minify path skipped it too, and it simply vanished. Found by an erase test that cut a hole and then could not find the object.
  • Cheap and complete because an object never reaches past its box's immediate neighbours, so the ring of eight is the whole of it. Asks each neighbour's own spatial index rather than scanning its objects, because this runs on every bake for eight boxes and a linear scan there is what a drag over a crowded document feels like.
  • Neighbouring origins differ by whole boxes, so the translation is exact, and nothing is minted just because a tile was looked at.
_solid(o, rec, rect)A tile-covering quad, overlapped into its neighbours.§8
ts._solid

Emits the tile-covering rectangle that stands in for a flooding object, overlapped into its neighbours by the seam pad.

_ensureDown · _bakeDown(F, i, j)The minify path. Every non-ancestor box at or below this depth, projected in one jump — safe at any distance because coordinates only shrink. Sub-pixel content is culled and near-threshold content is size-tagged for the fade.§9
ts._ensureDown

Returns a minify tile, building it when the cache misses, the epoch moved or `chainSeq` changed. The bake runs through `_bakeSettled` (F78).

ts._bakeDown

Builds one tile of finer and sideways ink minified into this frame. Candidates come from `_downSources`, in depth order.

  • A frame is skipped whole when even the largest possible object would be under the fade floor, or when its index's extent (`Document.frameExtent`) is under it or misses the tile. Per object: its size at this frame's deepest zoom (view-independent, so the verdict does not flicker) culls it below `fadeLoPx` and tags it for the fade; then a box test against the tile, one direct projection, and `_downPieces`.
  • One jump is safe here at any distance because minifying only shrinks coordinates.
_downPieces(...) divergenceOne minified piece clipped to one tile — and flattened to polygons. Safe only because such a tile is a leaf that nothing inherits.§9
ts._downPieces

Clips one minified object to one tile.

  • A resolved outline minifies exactly, so all that happens is a clip to the padded tile and a flatten at this level's display fidelity. Fills are clipped as rings with their winding preserved so holes stay holes; strokes are clipped as polylines with the line width added to the window so end caps land beyond the padded tile.
  • Stores polygons, not arcs — the one place the chain's exactness is not carried through. Safe for exactly one structural reason: a minify tile is a leaf. The chain reads the parent's magnify tiles and its objects, never its minify tiles, so a polygon made here can never be inherited or used as a boolean operand.
_onDoc · _removeObject
_addObject · _appendUp
_appendDown · _overlaps		Incremental patching: one edit is cheaper to patch in than to re-derive, so a tile is rebuilt only when correctness needs it.§9
ts._onDoc

Routes a document event to the cache: a reset clears it; a frame event (`refile`, `removeFrame`, `addFrame`, `mergeFrame`, `splitFrame`) goes to `_onFrameEvent`; a removal filters pieces out; an add or finalise patches pieces in, a live add waiting for its finalise.

  • A change marked `offsetsOnly` or `attrOnly` is ignored: a move changes nothing a tile is made of (F55). Any other change removes and re-adds.
ts._removeObject

Filters an object's pieces out of every cached tile, or in drag mode drops off-screen tiles outright.

ts._addObject

Patches one new object into every cached tile that should show it.

  • For a magnify tile: if the object's box is a direct parent, append it; if it is further up the chain, the tile's correctness depends on intermediate tiles too, so the tile is invalidated instead. A coarser off-branch object also invalidates, because the neighbour pickup is harder to patch precisely than to redo.
  • For a minify tile: append if the object is non-ancestor and at or below this depth.
ts._appendUp

Adds one object to one already-built magnify tile, using the same classify-and-derive path a full bake uses.

ts._appendDown

Adds one object to one already-built minify tile, re-running the size gate and the bounding-box cull first.

_evict · _evictPerLevelLeast-recently-used, globally and per frame, never touching what is on screen.§3
ts._evict

Evicts least-recently-used tiles down to the global cap, never touching anything currently on screen, then applies the per-box cap.

ts._evictPerLevel

The per-box half of eviction, so one busy box cannot consume the whole cache.

size · _tileKeysInspection. Test-facing.
ts.size

Cache size and keys. Test-facing only.

flattenAll(objs)Turns derived pieces' loops into stored Loops, so a cached tile holds eight doubles a piece.§7
ts.flattenAll

In place, and returns the list. The freeze and the chop hand over transient piece arrays; the cache keeps the `Loop` form the document's natives use.

TileStoreThe bidirectional tile cache.§6
ts.TileStore

Keyed by box. Everything shown from another level comes through here, and nothing else caches derived geometry.

_rerouteGroups(F)The moved objects to be read from another frame at F, grouped by source frame and remainder; memoised.§6
ts._rerouteGroups

Skips objects homed at F (natives, rendered live) and those homed deeper than F, which the residual draws. For the rest `LevelMap.objShift` names the source frame and remainder; objects sharing both form one group, so each tile is scanned once a group.

  • Memoised per frame on the document's `rev`, the lattice's `addrEpoch` and its frame count, for the last four frames; a key that changed during the walk is not kept. Measured: the walk was 70 ms of a 113-140 ms list build on the Magnum Opus (16,889 tables, jsdom).
_upPiecesOver(parentId, pr, only)The parent's magnified pieces over a rectangle, one square's copy of each object when the rectangle straddles squares.§9
ts._upPiecesOver

Inside one parent cache square: that square's up pieces. Across several: the square holding the rectangle's centre, and another square's piece of an object only when the centre square's clip does not cover the rectangle. `only` limits it to one object id; its one caller passes null.

  • Two squares' pieces are the same ink with clip vertices rounded on different rectangles, and 4,096x per crossing later the copies diverged by thousands of units (F42). The erase's descent cedes the same square by the same rule.
_downSources(F, rect)The frames a down tile of F reads: every non-ancestor at F's depth or deeper whose cell, grown by one, meets the tile.§9
ts._downSources

Walks F's subtree, then out through each ancestor into its other children's subtrees, carrying scale and offset into F's units; a subtree whose cell grown by one (REACH, invariant 2) misses the tile is skipped whole. Lists only frames with natives, counted with `Document.count`, which settles nothing. Ascending depth.

  • A native overhanging its frame's neighbours is not found, as with the ring pickup (DESIGN.md §9).
chainSeq(F)The sum of the address sequence numbers of F and its ancestors, stamped on every tile built at F.§6
ts.chainSeq

A tile built under an older sum read its content through an address a subtree move has since changed, and is rebuilt on its next lookup; no walk over the moved subtree is needed. Memoised per frame for one lattice `addrEpoch`.

_onFrameEvent(ev)A frame moved, was set aside, came back or merged: drops every cached tile its footprint touches, at the old address and the new.§6
ts._onFrameEvent

The footprint is the frame's cell grown by its subtree's reach (invariant 2), in the parent's units, at its current address (the recorded one for a merged frame) and, for a `refile`, its previous one; mapped into each cached tile's frame and tested against the tile padded by the seam pad. A merged frame's own tiles are deleted outright.

  • Tiles of the moved subtree itself go stale through `chainSeq`; a table change drops nothing (F55).
framesLeft(F)The camera has moved to frame F: drops every cached tile except F's ancestors', those just pinned by the camera's read, and the ladder's warm ones.§9
ts.framesLeft

Called by `_buildList` after its read, so the tiles `_reroute` read from other frames survive. Returns the count dropped.

  • Keeping the warm tiles is F83: dropping them re-baked cold the tiles the zoom that followed needed (measured 440 -> 64 ms for the first list in jsdom).

Renderer.js 1,354 lines

The SVG renderer, behind ?svg, and the base class of the raster one (layer 05, the paper), which keeps its live stroke, its lasso and its per-scene origin. One Two.js group per object kept in drawing order, and a per-frame difference. Decides nothing about what is visible.

Tells the drawing library to flush to the screen.

The wide-stroke gate: whether a stroke is painting wider than the limit now, whether it could ever within its level, and which representation it is currently using.

  • The gate is fidelity-neutral — raw stroking and the outline agree to well under display tolerance — so its value only trades safety against browser mis-stroking of enormous widths against the work of fitting outlines.
needsFatFlip · needsFadeFlip
hasPendingNearFat		When a camera-only frame is not enough. needsFadeFlip is the fix for the fading-piece defect: grouping is decided during a full render but fading depends on the live camera, so the camera-only path could reapply opacity without regrouping.§9 §16
rnd.needsFatFlip

Is a wide stroke approaching the point where raw stroking becomes unsafe, so it must flip to its outline form before the next frame?

rnd.needsFadeFlip

Has any piece crossed the fully-present line since its group was built?

  • Grouping is decided during a full render, but fade is a function of the live camera — so a zoom can invalidate the grouping without anything else changing, and a camera-only frame reapplies opacity without regrouping.
  • Without this the stale grouping simply persists: the member that should have left the family stays in it, and the whole family wears its fade. That is the defect where a cut-off piece faded out of existence while zooming.
rnd.hasPendingNearFat

Are wide strokes close enough to the gate that the engine should start fitting their outlines during idle time?

render(list, level)The per-frame difference. Group by object — or by family, when a family is fully present — compare signatures, rebuild only what changed, insert at the id-sorted position.§9
rnd.render

The per-frame difference. Rebuilds only what actually changed.

  • Groups the display list by object — or by family, when every member of a family is fully present rather than fading, so a multi-level object draws as one path and its pieces do not seam.
  • Builds a signature per group and compares it with the last one. Same signature means identical geometry, so the existing paths are reused and only the opacity is reapplied.
  • Rebuilt groups are inserted at their drawing-order position; vanished ids are removed.
  • Reports whether anything was reordered, and records how many groups were rebuilt — zero means a fully cached crossing.
syncCameraOnly()A pure camera move: one transform, plus opacity for faded groups. No geometry rebuild at all.§9
rnd.syncCameraOnly

A camera move with no geometry rebuild: write the world transform, and refresh opacity for the groups that fade, because fade depends on the live zoom.

syncWorld()Fold the scene's origin into the world transform in full precision, so the cancellation happens here and nothing large ever reaches the browser's lower-precision maths.§9
rnd.syncWorld

Writes the world transform, folding the scene's local origin into it in full precision.

  • Anchors are stored relative to a local origin so they stay small, and the bracketed translation is screen-sized whenever the view is near the content. The cancellation between the pan and the scaled origin happens here, in the engine's own arithmetic, where it is exact — nothing large ever reaches the drawing library's lower-precision matrices or the browser's rasterizer.
  • Also refreshes the debug overlays and the selection indicator, which all follow the same transform.

_opacityOf · _applyOpacity · _fadeThe continuous fade across the sub-pixel cull, so content shrinks out of existence smoothly rather than popping.§9
rnd._applyOpacity

Applies an object's opacity to its group, multiplied by the continuous fade.

  • Opacity lives on the group rather than the paths so that overlapping pieces of one object union before opacity applies, instead of double-darkening where they overlap.
rnd._fade

The continuous fade factor across the sub-pixel cull.

  • Converts a piece's tagged size into its actual on-screen size at the current zoom, and ramps linearly from fully transparent at the lower threshold to fully present at the upper one, so content shrinks out of existence smoothly rather than popping.
_sig(o, vw)A piece signature — same signature, same geometry, reuse the paths. Must include coordinates, not counts: scrolling the tile set by one swaps pieces without changing any count, and a count-only signature leaves stale paths on screen.§9
rnd._sig

A group's signature: same signature, same geometry, paths reused. It must include coordinates, not only counts: scrolling the tile set by one swaps pieces without changing any count.

  • A shape's part is its loop and piece counts and its bbox to two decimals, memoised per piece on `_ver`; the edit counter is in it because a pixel of drag at the deepest zoom is under the rounding. A fill uses its first and last points; a stroke its ends, width and representation (raw, outline, or pending past the gate).
  • A piece straddling the chop window carries the window's key, so a re-chop rebuilds exactly those groups; a piece with a residual carries it, since a drag from below moves it every event.
_buildPieces · _addFillPath
_addShapePath · _buildInto		Build a group's paths. A family's fills and resolved shapes go into one path, so coverage accumulates before anything composites and there is no seam to cover.§9
rnd._buildPieces

Builds a group's paths, merging every area piece (tile fills and resolved arc shapes) of one effective colour and opacity into a single path, in order; anything else flushes the bucket and goes through `_buildInto`.

  • Abutting paths seam: each covers part of the boundary pixel and composites in turn, measured at 18-25% toward white. Subpaths of one path do not, because coverage accumulates before compositing (DESIGN.md §9).
rnd._addFillPath

Adds an accumulated polygon path to a group, with its colour and opacity.

rnd._addShapePath

Adds an accumulated outline path to a group, with its colour and opacity.

rnd._buildInto

Builds one unmerged piece into a group. A shape goes through `_pushArea`: arcs by their plan, clipped to the chop window where it reaches past it. A stroke still carrying its pen's chain is drawn from that chain; a fat stroke as its curve-capsule outline (a pending one fitted within 12 ms a render); a fill as a polygon path; anything else as a stroked path, shifted by its residual.

  • Drawing the pen's own chain is what makes pen-up invisible: the ink under the pen, before the bake and after it are one curve.
_applyThinScale (static)The thin-object rescale. Chrome drops a filled path whose features are too small in the numbers handed over, however much the transform then enlarges them. Multiply the object's anchors by a power of two and divide its own group transform by the same — pixel-identical by construction.§9
rnd._applyThinScale

Rescales an object whose features are too small in the numbers handed over, however much the transform then enlarges them.

  • Chrome drops such a path entirely. Measured on the real geometry, holding the on-screen result pixel-identical and varying only the numbers: a feature 0.0657 units across renders and 0.0641 does not, while the app was handing over 0.0033.
  • The fix is a change of units for that object alone: multiply its anchors by a power of two and divide its own group's transform by the same number. Pixel-identical by construction, and applied at the end of the build so nothing upstream knows it happened.
  • It costs nothing in caching, because the numbers come from the level projection rather than the zoom and do not change as the camera moves.
ensureOutline · _buildOutlineIntoFat strokes as filled capsule outlines, fitted lazily and on approach rather than all at once.§9
addLive · setLiveArcs · endLiveThe in-progress stroke, drawn outside the diff so it is immediate — and drawn from the pen's own arc chain, so the ink does not change shape at pen-up and again when the outline lands.§7
rnd.addLive

Attaches the in-progress stroke to the scene, outside the difference pass, so it is immediate.

rnd.setLiveArcs

Redraws the in-progress stroke from the pen's current arc chain.

rnd.endLive

Detaches the in-progress stroke; the resolved object takes over.

perfRendererNow()Monotonic time for the render budget.§9
rnd.perfRendererNow

Monotonic time for the render budget.

RendererThe SVG renderer, behind `?svg`, and the base class the raster renderer extends.§9
rnd.Renderer

Owns the Two.js scene: one persistent group per object id sorted by (z, id), the per-frame diff by signature, retained per-level scenes, the per-scene origin and chop window, the live pen path, and the lasso and selection-indicator layers.

  • `RasterRenderer` subclasses it, drawing the ink into plates and keeping the live stroke and the chevrons from here (DESIGN.md §9). The engine's own default is this renderer, so the suites and the one-off engines are SVG.
_syncWorldTransform()Writes the world group's scale and translation, folding the scene origin in at float64.§9
rnd._syncWorldTransform

`translation = inPan + inScale * origin`: anchors are origin-relative, and the cancellation between the pan and the scaled origin happens here in doubles, so nothing large reaches Two.js's float32 matrices or the browser (DESIGN.md §9). `RasterRenderer` overrides it to take the snapped translation from its view.

_chopHolds(chop)Whether a scene's chop window still holds: the view inside its inner half, the zoom under 4x the zoom it was chosen at.§9
rnd._chopHolds

Whether a scene's chop window still holds: the view inside its inner half, the zoom under 4x the zoom it was chosen at.

needsWindowChop()Tells the engine a camera-only frame must become a full render, because the view has left its chop window's budget.§9
rnd.needsWindowChop

False mid-stroke (the live path's anchors must not move under the pen) and with the chop off. The full render chooses a new window and rebuilds only the groups that straddle it, before the old edge can reach the screen (F40). `RasterRenderer` returns false.

_maybeRechop(sc)Chooses the scene's chop window afresh, centred on the view, when it has none or the last no longer holds.§9
rnd._maybeRechop

The window is +-`_chopPx` device px (2^18 for the default config) at the current zoom, under a new key. Nothing is rebuilt here: the key enters the signature of every piece that straddles the window, and the diff rebuilds exactly those.

_chopFor(o)The chop window an area piece must be clipped to, or null when it can go to the browser whole.§9
rnd._chopFor

Null for a piece inside the window or wholly outside it (hundreds of screens off, where what the browser makes of far coordinates cannot show), and for anything but a shape or a fill. A tile piece is settled first by the rectangle it was cut on; otherwise by its bounds, a pass over a fill's points. A piece with a residual is judged against the window shifted back. Memoised per render: the signature asks, then the build.

_pushArea(verts, o, og)Appends one area piece, a shape's arcs or a fill's rings, as anchors, clipped to the chop window where it reaches past it.§9
rnd._pushArea

The residual is folded into the origin the anchors are taken against, and the window shifted to match, so the piece's geometry is untouched. A shape is cut by `shapeLoopsInRect` (exact on arcs; the window quad when the window lies wholly inside the ink), a fill by `clipRingsToRect`. The cut exists only in this build; the selection indicator and the erase overlay read the whole piece.

_planFor(o)The arc plan for one piece: the frame's constants plus the piece's clip rectangle, so its seams are known.§9
rnd._planFor

A covering quad (classifyUp's solid tier) takes the plan with no length split: its edges are the tile's own, overlapped by the neighbours.

Stage.js 1,448 lines

The scene both renderers draw (DESIGN.md §9): the camera frame's items in paint order, kept from the document's and the tile cache's own events so it is never behind the document; the generation G every commit moves; and the freshness of every plate cell the store holds or has in flight (`dirtySince`). A drag writes nothing: its held natives are drawn, hit and lassoed at their placement plus the pointer's delta.

FunctionWhat it does in the design§

placementModel.js 173 lines

The document model as the Stage reads it (A1 §6): which natives a frame draws live, where a native's picture is seen from a frame, which natives are drawn away from their stored bits, and a frame's footprint. One composition — a native's own table plus its home frame's shift — and no read settles, mints or changes a table.

FunctionWhat it does in the design§

05 The paper

The raster renderer, the app's default: the render list rastered into cached plates by our own coverage rasteriser, off the main thread

raster/RasterRenderer.js 1,382 lines

The raster renderer, the app's default: a `Renderer` subclass that draws the ink into plates through `PictureLayer`, `PlateStore` and the worker pool, and keeps only the live stroke and the selection chevrons in SVG. It is the only poster of raster jobs, and it runs the drag plane, the pen-up hold, the crossing prebake, the zoom-out ladder and the Scenes snapshots (DESIGN.md §9).

FunctionWhat it does in the design§
resetRasterStats()Zeroes every counter in `rasterStats`, the renderer's own report counters.§15
rr.resetRasterStats

Zeroes every counter in `rasterStats`, the renderer's own report counters.

RasterRendererThe raster renderer: a `Renderer` subclass that paints the render list into cached plates on a canvas instead of into SVG.§9
rr.RasterRenderer

It keeps the base class's Two.js `<svg>` for the live stroke and the selection chevrons only; the ink goes through `PictureLayer` (the mapping and the compose), `PlateStore` (the cache and its invalidation) and `rasterWorkerClient` (the queue and the workers). It is the only module that posts raster jobs.

  • The app's default renderer since 2026-09-22; the SVG renderer is behind `?svg`. The engine's own `raster` option defaults to off, so the suites and the one-off engines are SVG (DESIGN.md §9).
RasterRenderer.constructor(container, camera, cfg, opts)Builds the SVG base, the `PictureLayer`, the drag plane and the counters, attaches the perf recorder and spawns the worker pool.§9
rr.RasterRenderer.constructor

Positions the Two.js `<svg>` absolutely at z-index 1 (ink canvas 0, ant canvas 2, chevrons 3), reads the dpr, builds the layer with its `onPlates` and `onRepost` callbacks routed to `_post`, hooks the store's `onRelease`, creates the `MovePlane`, attaches `rasterPerf` to its seven sources, arms the dpr listener and calls `ensureRasterPool`.

  • It also forwards the store's `onShow` (the tab visible again) to the engine's `onShown`, and sets `forcePerStepDrag`, a test hook that turns the drag plane off so every drag renders each step.
  • The camera must be the same object the engine later hands `frameFor`: the settle's publish and the quantum switch read the injected one outside the animation-frame cycle. The engine constructs the `PlateStore` and owns its lifetime.
_buildSelOverlay(svg)Builds the one SVG selection layer the raster path needs, `bl-sel-edges` for the chevrons, at z-index 3.§12
rr._buildSelOverlay

The ants are painted on `OverlayLayer`'s canvas, so `bl-sel-layer` is never created. `_selOv` and `_selEls` keep the base class's shape, so `Renderer._dropSelOverlay` and `_renderSelChevrons` run unchanged.

antPainter (getter)True: tells `overlays._selDecide` to keep each ant run's pieces for the canvas painter instead of building an SVG path string.§12
rr.antPainter

The code records 8.3 ms and 345 KB taken off a decision at F39's density.

_renderSelOverlay(view)Draws the selection indicator on the raster path: the ants on the overlay canvas, the chevrons in SVG, both at the published view.§12
rr._renderSelOverlay

Asks the engine for its decision (`_selAntsFn`), timing it as the overlay's `decideMs`; with nothing to show it drops the overlay. Otherwise it sizes `bl-sel-edges`, builds the `OverlayLayer` on first use, hands it the decision, the view and `_edgeShift`, draws the chevrons with `Renderer._renderSelChevrons` and keeps the edge layer last in the host.

  • It takes the published view, never the camera, so the ants and the ink share one mapping. With no view published yet it leaves what is drawn.
_dropSelOverlay()Hides the ant canvas and removes the SVG chevron layer when the selection goes.§12
rr._dropSelOverlay

The overlay's buffer is kept, so the next selection does not reallocate it.

_makeOverlay()Creates the `OverlayLayer` for the ants on the first selection decision and adds it to the renderer's list of screen layers.§12
rr._makeOverlay

Never at construction: a tool change must not cost the plane's 10.48 MiB. Joining `_layers` is what has it resized, released and destroyed with the ink layer. It also arms the reduced-motion listener.

_edgeShift(view)The CSS-px difference between the published view's snapped translation and the camera's pan, applied to the screen-edge ant spans.§12
rr._edgeShift

The edge spans are computed in the camera's screen px while the ink is composed at the view's whole-pixel translation; the overlay adds this to the spans only. One two-element array, reused.

_armReducedMotion()Listens to `prefers-reduced-motion` and passes it to the ant overlay, which owns the crawl clock.§12
rr._armReducedMotion

A CSS rule cannot stop the canvas crawl; the chevrons keep the stylesheet's own rule. A no-op without `matchMedia` (jsdom), which is what lets a raster engine construct there.

_dropReducedMotion()Removes the reduced-motion listener.§12
rr._dropReducedMotion

Removes the reduced-motion listener.

setSize(w, h)Resizes the SVG base and every screen layer at the current devicePixelRatio, and re-arms the dpr listener.§9

The base `setSize` carries no dpr and the layers take `(w, h, dpr)`, so this is the one place that reads `devicePixelRatio`.

_armDpr(dpr)Listens for a devicePixelRatio change, which fires no `resize`, and resizes the layers when one happens.§9
rr._armDpr

`matchMedia("(resolution: Ndppx)")` matches one ratio, so the query is re-armed at the new ratio on each `setSize`. The case is a window dragged to a second monitor. A no-op without `matchMedia`.

_dropDpr()Removes the dpr listener.§9
rr._dropDpr

Removes the dpr listener.
